tamil:
பொருளல் லவரைப் பொருளாகச் செய்யும்
பொருளல்லது இல்லை பொருள்.
transliteration:
Porulal lavaraip porulaakach cheyyum
porulalladhu illai porul.
current_meaning: Nothing but wealth can turn people who count for nothing into people who count for something; there is no other thing like it.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a boy nobody picks for the team. One day he brings a brand-new football, and suddenly everyone wants to play with him. He is the same boy, but now people notice him. Valluvar says money works like that ball: it makes people who were ignored get noticed.
university_explanation: The chapter opens the Kural’s treatment of koozh (கூழ், treasury or wealth), one of the six limbs of the state named in kural 381, and it begins with a deliberately startling claim. The couplet plays on three senses of porul: ‘thing of account’, ‘worth’, and ‘wealth’, so that porulallavar are ‘those who are no-thing’, and the second line says there is no porul (thing) except porul (wealth). Parimelazhagar treats the verse as a plain statement of how the world behaves rather than a moral endorsement, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar likewise read it as a description of social esteem, not of true merit. The ytamizh text divides பொருளல்லது இல்லை, while the sandhi-joined text at thirukkural-thamizh reads பொருளல்ல தில்லை; the words are the same.

tamil:
இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர் செல்வரை
எல்லாரும் செய்வர் சிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Illaarai ellaarum elluvar selvarai
ellaarum seyvar sirappu.
current_meaning: Everyone looks down on those who have nothing, and everyone honours those who are rich.
elementary_explanation: Two children come to a party. One wears a torn shirt and the other a shiny new outfit. Some people smile at the second child and ignore the first, even though nothing else is different. Valluvar is telling us this happens, so that we notice it and do not treat people unfairly.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a tight parallelism: illaarai (the have-nots) against selvarai (the wealthy), and ellaarum elluvar (all scorn) against ellaarum seyvar sirappu (all do honour). Mu. Varadarasanar adds in parentheses that the poor are scorned even if they have other virtues and the rich honoured even if they have none, which makes the verse a comment on injustice as well as a fact of life. Parimelazhagar reads it, like 751, as a reason for the ruler to gather wealth: a king without a treasury would suffer the same contempt. Kalaignar’s gloss calls this simply the way of the world (உலக நடப்பு). The sandhi-joined text reads இல்லாரை யெல்லாரு மெள்ளுவர், which divides into the same words.

tamil:
பொருளென்னும் பொய்யா விளக்கம் இருளறுக்கும்
எண்ணிய தேயத்துச் சென்று.
transliteration:
Porulennum poyyaa vilakkam irularukkum
enniya theyaththuch chendru.
current_meaning: Wealth is a lamp that never fails: carried into any land its owner chooses, it cuts through the darkness there, above all the darkness of hostility.
elementary_explanation: Think of a torch that never runs out of batteries. Wherever you walk at night, it lights the path. Valluvar says money can be like that: when you go to a new place, it can help you make friends and solve problems.
university_explanation: The metaphor pairs poyyaa vilakkam (the lamp that does not fail or lie) with iruL (darkness), and the second line sends the lamp to enniya theyam, ‘the country one has in mind’ (theyam from Sanskrit desha). Parimelazhagar glosses the darkness as enmity (பகையாகிய இருள்), and Pope and Drew’s English follows him with ‘the darkness (of enmity)’; Solomon Pappaiah likewise says wealth enters even foreign lands and dispels the darkness of hostility. Mu. Varadarasanar reads iruL more broadly as any obstacle (இடையூறு), and Kalaignar as suffering (துன்பம்). The verse sets up 759, where wealth becomes the sharpest weapon against a foe’s pride. The sandhi-joined text reads விளக்க மிருளறுக்கு மெண்ணிய, which divides into the same words.

tamil:
அறன்ஈனும் இன்பமும் ஈனும் திறனறிந்து
தீதின்றி வந்த பொருள்.
transliteration:
Aran eenum inbamum eenum thiranarindhu
theedhindri vandha porul.
current_meaning: Wealth gained by knowing the right ways and without doing wrong gives birth to both virtue and happiness.
elementary_explanation: Imagine two children selling lemonade. One makes it carefully and charges a fair price. The other sneaks sugar from a neighbour and cheats customers. Only the first can enjoy the money without worry and use it to do kind things. Valluvar says honest money brings both goodness and happiness.
university_explanation: The verb eenum (ஈனும், ‘brings forth, gives birth to’) is repeated for both aram (virtue) and inbam (pleasure or happiness), so wealth is pictured as the parent of the other two purusharthas. The conditions are thiran arindhu, ‘knowing the proper means’, and theedhu indri, ‘without evil’. Parimelazhagar takes the proper means to be those fitting one’s station and the law, and the absence of evil to mean acquiring without harm or deceit to others. Sivayogi Sivakumar adds that it means seeking wealth with knowledge of one’s own ability and harming no one. The sandhi-joined text reads அறனீனு மின்பமு மீனுந், which divides into the same words.

tamil:
அருளொடும் அன்பொடும் வாராப் பொருளாக்கம்
புல்லார் புரள விடல்.
transliteration:
Arulodum anbodum vaaraap porulaakkam
pullaar purala vidal.
current_meaning: Wealth that does not come together with compassion and love should not be embraced; let it roll away.
elementary_explanation: Suppose you could win a big prize, but only by being mean to a friend. Valluvar says to let that prize go. Money that makes you unkind is like a shiny apple that is rotten inside.
university_explanation: The first line names two qualities the earning must carry: arul (அருள், compassion toward all beings, the subject of chapter 25) and anbu (அன்பு, affection toward one’s own, the subject of chapter 8). The second line is vivid: pullaar, ‘not embracing’ (from pullu, to hug or cling), and purala vidal, ‘letting it roll off’, as one lets go of something that slips from the arms. Parimelazhagar applies the verse to the ruler, who should refuse revenue gathered by cruelty to his subjects, and Pope and Drew’s English accordingly begins with ‘(Kings) should rather avoid’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah generalise it to anyone who earns. The sandhi-joined text reads அருளொடு மன்பொடும், which divides into the same words.

tamil:
உறுபொருளும் உல்கு பொருளும்தன் ஒன்னார்த்
தெறுபொருளும் வேந்தன் பொருள்.
transliteration:
Uruporulum ulgu porulumthan onnaarth
theruporulum vendhan porul.
current_meaning: Wealth that comes to the crown without an owner, revenue from customs and tolls, and tribute taken from defeated enemies: these are the king’s wealth.
elementary_explanation: Think of a school fund. It gets money from lost-and-found items nobody claims, from small fees for using the playground, and from the prize when the school wins a match against another school. Valluvar lists the kinds of money that belong to a king’s treasury in a similar way.
university_explanation: This is the chapter’s one technical verse, listing three lawful sources of royal revenue. Uruporul is ‘wealth that comes of itself’, which Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah explain as ownerless property such as heirless estates and treasure trove, while Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take it as ordinary tax (இறை, வரி). Ulgu porul is customs or toll revenue on goods, and theru porul is tribute or spoil taken from subdued enemies (onnaar). The verse spells out what 755 means in practice: a king’s legitimate income has clear, lawful channels. The sandhi-joined text reads உறுபொருளு முல்கு பொருளுந்தன் னொன்னார்த், which divides into the same words.

tamil:
அருளென்னும் அன்பீன் குழவி பொருளென்னும்
செல்வச் செவிலியால் உண்டு.
transliteration:
Arulennum anbeen kuzhavi porulennum
selvach cheviliyaal undu.
current_meaning: Compassion is the child that love gives birth to, and it is raised by the rich foster-mother called wealth.
elementary_explanation: Picture a baby born to a loving mother, cared for by a kind nanny who has plenty of food and warm blankets. Valluvar says kindness is like that baby: love gives birth to it, and money helps it grow, because it is easier to help others when you have something to give.
university_explanation: This is one of the Kural’s finest extended metaphors. Arul (compassion for all beings) is the kuzhavi, the infant, born of anbu (love for one’s own; anbeen is anbu plus eenra, ‘borne by love’), and porul is the selvach cheviliyal, the rich wet-nurse or foster-mother (cevili) who raises it. The genealogy reverses the usual worry that wealth corrupts: love begets compassion, but compassion cannot grow into practical kindness without means. It links back to chapter 8, Anbudaimai, which says love begets affection and friendship, and it answers 755 by showing the right relation of wealth to arul and anbu. The sandhi-joined text reads அருளென்னு மன்பீன் குழவி பொருளென்னுஞ், which divides into the same words.

tamil:
குன்றேறி யானைப்போர் கண்டற்றால் தன்கைத்தொன்று
உண்டாகச் செய்வான் வினை.
transliteration:
Kundreri yaanaippor kandatraal thankaiththondru
undaagach cheyvaan vinai.
current_meaning: Someone who starts a venture with money already in hand is like a person watching an elephant fight from a hilltop, safe and able to see everything.
elementary_explanation: Imagine two huge elephants pushing and fighting in a field. If you stood in the middle, you could get hurt. But if you climb a hill and watch from the top, you are safe and can see everything. Valluvar says that starting a big job with savings in your pocket is like watching from that hill.
university_explanation: The simile draws on a familiar sight in Sangam India, the royal elephant fight, which was deadly to anyone on the ground and a pleasure to watch from high up. Thankaiththu ondru undaaga means ‘with something being in one’s own hand’, that is, having one’s own funds, and cheyvaan vinai is ‘the work of one who acts’. Parimelazhagar explains that such a person has no need to depend on others and so can watch the struggle of the undertaking without fear, while Kalaignar adds the image of not being caught between the fighting elephants. The sandhi-joined text reads கண்டற்றாற் றன்கைத்தொன் றுண்டாகச், which divides into the same words.

tamil:
செய்க பொருளைச் செறுநர் செருக்கறுக்கும்
எஃகதனிற் கூரிய தில்.
transliteration:
Seyga porulaich cherunar serukkarukkum
eqkadhanir kooriya thil.
current_meaning: Build up wealth: there is no steel sharper than it for cutting down the pride of your enemies.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a bully who brags that nobody can stand up to him. Then the whole class saves up to build a strong new fence and hire a coach, and suddenly the bully stops bragging. Valluvar says a well-stocked treasury is the sharpest sword against a proud enemy.
university_explanation: The verse opens with a blunt imperative, seyga porulai, ‘make wealth!’, which is rare in the Kural and gives the command its force. Cherunar are foes, serukku is their arrogance, and aRukkum (‘that cuts off’) sets up the image of eqku (எஃகு), steel or a sword, of which nothing is sharper (kooriyadhu il). Parimelazhagar explains that wealth lets a king raise and keep armies and allies, and so humbles enemies without his having to strike himself. Solomon Pappaiah addresses the verse to anyone who wants to achieve something. The sandhi-joined text reads செருக்கறுக்கு மெஃகதனிற், which divides into the same words.

tamil:
ஒண்பொருள் காழ்ப்ப இயற்றியார்க்கு எண்பொருள்
ஏனை இரண்டும் ஒருங்கு.
transliteration:
Onporul kaazhppa iyatriyaarkku enporul
enai irandum orungu.
current_meaning: For those who have built up an abundance of good, honestly earned wealth, the other two aims of life, virtue and happiness, come together easily.
elementary_explanation: Think of a garden. Once the soil is rich and well watered, flowers and vegetables both grow easily. Valluvar says honest wealth is like that rich soil: once you have it, goodness and happiness grow easily too.
university_explanation: The closing verse ties the chapter to the three aims of life (muppaal: aram, porul, inbam) that give the Kural its three books. Onporul is ‘bright’ or excellent wealth, which the commentators take to mean wealth gained by good means, echoing 754; kaazhppa (from kaazh, hard core) means firmly and abundantly; enporul is ‘an easy thing’ (en, easy); and enai irandum orungu means ‘the other two, together’. Parimelazhagar explains that for such a person virtue and pleasure are both easily attained, and Kalaignar names the three purusharthas explicitly. The verse repeats the pairing in 754 and closes the chapter’s argument that honestly earned wealth underpins a complete life. The sandhi-joined text reads இயற்றியார்க் கெண்பொரு ளேனை யிரண்டு மொருங்கு, which divides into the same words.

tamil:
உறுப்பமைந்து ஊறஞ்சா வெல்படை வேந்தன்
வெறுக்கையுள் எல்லாம் தலை.
transliteration:
Uruppamaindhu ooranjaa velpadai vendhan
verukkaiyul ellaam thalai.
current_meaning: An army that is complete in all its parts and wins without fearing wounds is the foremost of all the treasures a king possesses.
elementary_explanation: Think of a school sports team where every position is filled, everyone has practised, and nobody is scared of a hard game. A coach would say that team is worth more than any trophy cupboard. Valluvar says a king’s well-prepared army is like that: his most precious possession.
university_explanation: The chapter opens the Padai-iyal (the section on the army), and its first couplet ranks the army above every other form of veṟukkai (வெறுக்கை, ‘wealth, treasure’). Uṟuppu (உறுப்பு, ‘limb’) is read by Parimelazhagar as the traditional four limbs of an Indian army, elephants, chariots, horse and foot, so uṟuppamaintu means ‘complete in its divisions’; ūṟu (ஊறு) is ‘wound’ or ‘harm’, and ūṟañcā ‘not dreading injury’. The logic echoes kural 381, which lists the army (படை) first among the six limbs of a kingdom, and the Arthashastra’s list of seven elements of sovereignty. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss the line almost identically; Solomon Pappaiah modernizes the ‘limbs’ as land, sea and air forces and police. The ytamizh and thirukkural-thamizh texts agree, differing only in sandhi (உறுப்பமைந் தூறஞ்சா).

tamil:
உலைவிடத்து ஊறஞ்சா வன்கண் தொலைவிடத்துத்
தொல்படைக் கல்லால் அரிது.
transliteration:
Ulaividaththu ooranjaa vankan tholaividaththuth
tholpadaik kallaal aridhu.
current_meaning: The courage to stand firm in defeat, unafraid of injury even when the ranks have thinned, is rarely found in anything but a long-established army.
elementary_explanation: When a team is losing badly, new players often give up, but players who have trained together for years keep going. They have been through hard games before. Valluvar says an old, experienced army is like that: it keeps its courage even when things are going wrong.
university_explanation: Ulaivu (உலைவு) means ‘reverse, setback’ and tolaivu (தொலைவு) ‘diminution, loss of numbers’, so the couplet describes valour (vaṉkaṇ, வன்கண்) that survives both defeat and attrition. Tolpaṭai (தொல்படை, ‘ancient army’) is read by Parimelazhagar as the hereditary core force (often called மூலப்படை in the commentarial tradition), as against hired or allied troops, a distinction that closely parallels Kautilya’s preference for hereditary troops. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar follow this reading, while Solomon Pappaiah extends tolpaṭai to native citizen-soldiers whose families have long lived in the land. The text is identical in both sources apart from sandhi (வன்கண் டொலைவிடத்துத் in the joined text).

tamil:
ஒலித்தக்கால் என்னாம் உவரி எலிப்பகை
நாகம் உயிர்ப்பக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Oliththakkaal ennaam uvari elippakai
naagam uyirppak kedum.
current_meaning: What does it matter if a host of rats roars like the sea? At a single breath of the cobra they are scattered and ruined.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a crowd of mice squeaking very loudly in a barn. It sounds scary, but the moment a snake hisses, they all scurry away. Valluvar says a big, noisy army with no real courage is like those mice, and a small, brave army is like the snake.
university_explanation: The couplet is a celebrated uvamai (simile): uvari (உவரி, ‘the salt sea’) describes the roar of a vast but timid enemy, while nākam (நாகம், ‘cobra’) and uyirppa (உயிர்ப்ப, ‘as it breathes, hisses’) picture a small force of real valour. Parimelazhagar reads it as a statement that numbers without courage count for nothing against a brave army, and Solomon Pappaiah explicitly makes the cobra a small army and the rats a large one ‘rat-like in mind’. Kalaignar applies it to a single hero rising in anger. The text is the same in both sources apart from sandhi (ஒலித்தக்கா லென்னா முவரி யெலிப்பகை).

tamil:
அழிவின்றி அறைபோகா தாகி வழிவந்த
வன்க ணதுவே படை.
transliteration:
Azhivindri araipogaa thaagi vazhivandha
vankanadhuve padai.
current_meaning: That alone is an army which has not been destroyed, cannot be bought over by the enemy, and carries a courage handed down through generations.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a family that has played in the same village band for generations. Nobody could pay them to play for a rival band, and they never give up halfway through a parade. Valluvar says a true army is like that: loyal, steady, and brave because bravery runs in its history.
university_explanation: Three marks define the true army here: aḻiviṉmai (not being broken in battle), aṟaipōkāmai (அறைபோகாமை, not being undermined or won over by enemy intrigue, i.e. free of treachery and desertion), and vaḻivanta vaṉkaṇ (வழிவந்த வன்கண், valour inherited through lineage). Parimelazhagar takes aṟaipōtal as being corrupted by the enemy’s secret approaches, and Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as ‘not falling prey to the enemy’s deceit’. There is a small textual variant: ytamizh prints அழிவின்றி, while the sandhi-joined thirukkural-thamizh text reads அழிவின் றறைபோகா, i.e. அழிவின்று; the sense, ‘without destruction’, is unchanged.

tamil:
கூற்றுடன்று மேல்வரினும் கூடி எதிர்நிற்கும்
ஆற்ற லதுவே படை.
transliteration:
Kootrudandru melvarinum koodi edhirnirkum
aatraladhuve padai.
current_meaning: That alone is an army which has the strength to stand together and face the foe even if Death himself should come against it in fury.
elementary_explanation: Picture a group of friends holding hands in a line during a strong wind on the beach. Alone, each might be pushed over, but together they stay standing. Valluvar says a real army stands together like that, even against the scariest danger.
university_explanation: Kūṟṟu (கூற்று) is Death personified, identified by commentators with Yama, and uṭaṉṟu (உடன்று) means ‘having become enraged’. The key word is kūṭi (கூடி, ‘together, united’): the excellence praised is collective resolve rather than individual heroism, and āṟṟal (ஆற்றல்) is the strength to hold. Parimelazhagar notes that even the god of death cannot be resisted by ordinary means, so the hyperbole stresses unity as the army’s defining power. The two sources agree apart from sandhi (கூடி யெதிர்நிற்கு / மாற்ற லதுவே).

tamil:
மறமானம் மாண்ட வழிச்செலவு தேற்றம்
எனநான்கே ஏமம் படைக்கு.
transliteration:
Maramaanam maanda vazhichchelavu thetram
enanaange emam padaikku.
current_meaning: Valour, honour, following the noble path of those who went before, and being trusted: these four alone are an army’s safeguard.
elementary_explanation: A good scout troop needs four things: brave members, members who care about doing the right thing, members who follow the good habits of older scouts, and a leader who can trust them. Valluvar says an army needs the same four things to stay safe and strong.
university_explanation: The couplet names four qualities: maṟam (மறம், valour), māṉam (மானம், honour, sense of shame at disgrace), māṇṭa vaḻiccelavu (மாண்ட வழிச்செலவு, walking the excellent path of predecessors), and tēṟṟam (தேற்றம்). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar take tēṟṟam as ‘being trusted (tested and found reliable) by the king’, while Sivayogi Sivakumar renders it as ‘clear resolve’, a genuine interpretive divergence. Ēmam (ஏமம்) means ‘protection, safeguard’, and the emphatic nāṉkē (‘these four alone’) makes the list exclusive. Both sources agree on the wording (சந்தி: தேற்ற / மெனநான்கே யேமம்).

tamil:
தார்தாங்கிச் செல்வது தானை தலைவந்த
போர்தாங்கும் தன்மை அறிந்து.
transliteration:
Thaarthaangich chelvadhu thaanai thalaivandha
poarthaangum thanmai arindhu.
current_meaning: A true army knows how to withstand the attack that comes upon it, and so advances bearing the brunt of the enemy’s vanguard.
elementary_explanation: In a game of tug-of-war, the strongest kids stand at the front where the pull is hardest, and they know how to dig their heels in. Valluvar says a good army is like that: it knows how to take the first hard push and keep moving forward.
university_explanation: Tār (தார்) is the vanguard, called tūci (தூசி) in the commentaries, which Pope rendered ‘dust-van’ after the dust raised by an advancing force; tāṉai (தானை) is the army. Parimelazhagar reads the couplet as describing an army that, knowing the art of checking an oncoming assault (talaivanta pōr tāṅkum taṉmai), meets and bears the enemy’s vanguard. Solomon Pappaiah reads tār more broadly as the front-line foot soldiers, while Sivayogi Sivakumar takes it as an image of ranks arrayed like a banana bunch, an idiosyncratic reading. Both texts agree (சந்தி: போர்தாங்குந் தன்மை யறிந்து).

tamil:
அடல்தகையும் ஆற்றலும் இல்லெனினும் தானை
படைத்தகையால் பாடு பெறும்.
transliteration:
Adalthagaiyum aatralum illeninum thaanai
padaiththagaiyaal paadu perum.
current_meaning: Even if it lacks the power to attack and the strength to resist, an army can win renown by the splendour of its array and equipment.
elementary_explanation: A marching band in smart uniforms, all in step, can make a whole crowd stop and stare, even before it plays a note. Valluvar says an army that is neatly lined up and well equipped can earn respect just by how it looks and moves.
university_explanation: Aṭaltakai (அடல்தகை) is the capacity to attack and destroy, āṟṟal (ஆற்றல்) the capacity to withstand; paṭaittakai (படைத்தகை) is the excellence of the army’s equipment and array, and pāṭu (பாடு) means ‘renown, dignity’. Parimelazhagar understands the couplet as saying that order and splendour alone can deter or impress an enemy, and Solomon Pappaiah stresses the disciplined beauty of its formation. Kalaignar reads it slightly differently, as saying the array should be even more excellent than attack and defence. The two sources agree (சந்தி: அடல்தகையு மாற்றலு மில்லெனினுந் தானை).

tamil:
சிறுமையும் செல்லாத் துனியும் வறுமையும்
இல்லாயின் வெல்லும் படை.
transliteration:
Sirumaiyum sellaath thuniyum varumaiyum
illaayin vellum padai.
current_meaning: An army will win if it is free from dwindling numbers, from lasting discontent, and from want.
elementary_explanation: A team does best when nobody keeps quitting, nobody is sulking and angry at the coach, and everyone has enough food and kit. Valluvar says an army is the same: keep it whole, happy and well supplied, and it will win.
university_explanation: Three defects are named: ciṟumai (சிறுமை, diminution, a shrinking of numbers or strength), cellāt tuṉi (செல்லாத் துனி, a resentment that will not go away, which Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar direct specifically against the king or commander), and vaṟumai (வறுமை, poverty, i.e. unpaid or ill-supplied troops). Solomon Pappaiah follows this reading, while Sivayogi Sivakumar renders ciṟumai as ‘confusion’, a looser gloss. The couplet’s realism about morale and pay matches Kautilya’s detailed discussion of an army’s ‘calamities’. Both sources agree (சந்தி: சிறுமையுஞ் ... வறுமையு / மில்லாயின்).

tamil:
நிலைமக்கள் சால உடைத்தெனினும் தானை
தலைமக்கள் இல்வழி இல்.
transliteration:
Nilaimakkal saala udaiththeninum thaanai
thalaimakkal ilvazhi il.
current_meaning: Though an army has a great many steadfast soldiers, it cannot stand where there are no worthy leaders.
elementary_explanation: A choir may have lots of good singers, but without a conductor they start and stop at different times and it sounds like a mess. Valluvar says an army is the same: many brave soldiers are not enough without a good leader.
university_explanation: Nilaimakkaḷ (நிலைமக்கள்) are ‘steadfast men’, read by Parimelazhagar as long-serving, permanent soldiers, and cāla (சால) means ‘in abundance’; talaimakkaḷ (தலைமக்கள்) are the ‘head-men’, i.e. commanders or generals. The final il vaḻi il (இல்வழி இல்) is a terse play: ‘where they are not, (the army) is not’, which Mu. Varadarasanar glosses as the army having no glory and Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar as its not being able to hold its ground. The couplet closes the chapter by turning from the troops to their leadership, preparing for the next chapter, Paṭaiccerukku (படைச்செருக்கு, the martial pride of warriors). Both sources agree (சந்தி: சால வுடைத்தெனினுந் ... தலைமக்க ளில்வழி யில்).

tamil:
என்னைமுன் நில்லன்மின் தெவ்விர் பலரென்னை
முன்நின்று கல்நின் றவர்.
transliteration:
Ennaimun nillanmin thevvir palarennai
Munnindru kalnin Ravar.
current_meaning: A warrior calls out to the enemy: do not stand against my lord, for many who once stood before him now stand only as memorial stones.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a champion team whose fans warn the visitors: “Lots of teams came here thinking they would win, and now their names are just on the list of teams we beat.” The warrior is proud of his leader in the same way, and the proud words themselves are meant to make the other side think twice.
university_explanation: The chapter title padaiccherukku joins padai (army) and serukku (pride, exultant spirit), and this opening couplet is cast as a battlefield vaunt addressed to thevvir (“you enemies”). Parimelazhagar takes ennai not as “me” but as en + ai, “my lord” (ai = master, chief), so the soldier boasts of his commander rather than of himself; some modern renderings (e.g., Sivayogi Sivakumar on ytamizh.com) read it as the speaker’s own challenge. The punning repetition of nil- / nin- turns on “standing”: those who stood (nindru) against the lord now stand as kal (stone), alluding to the nadukal, the hero-stone erected for fallen warriors, a custom described in the Tolkappiyam’s Purattinai and attested in Sangam puram poetry. Both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give the couplet identically; the sandhi split “கல்நின் றவர்” = kal ninravar.

tamil:
கான முயலெய்த அம்பினில் யானை
பிழைத்தவேல் ஏந்தல் இனிது.
transliteration:
Kaana muyaleydha ambinil yaanai
Pizhaiththavel endhal inidhu.
current_meaning: It is better to hold a spear that missed an elephant than an arrow that killed a forest hare.
elementary_explanation: Would you rather say you beat a little kid at chess, or that you lost a close game to the school champion? Trying something truly hard, even if you miss, is more honourable than an easy win over someone weak.
university_explanation: The couplet contrasts kaana muyal (the hare of the forest, a small and timid quarry) with yaanai (the elephant, the most formidable target of ancient Tamil warfare), and the arrow (ambu) that succeeded against the hare with the spear (vel) that failed against the elephant (pizhaiththa vel). The key verb endhal, “to hold, to bear,” makes the line about what a warrior is proud to carry: honour belongs to the scale of the attempt, not merely its outcome. Parimelazhagar reads the hare and elephant as figures for weak and mighty enemies, so the teaching concerns the choice of a worthy adversary. Kalaignar’s modern gloss states the point directly: aiming at the strong and missing outranks aiming at the weak and hitting. Both base texts agree on the wording; the sandhi form முயலெய்த = muyal eydha.

tamil:
பேராண்மை என்ப தறுகண்ஒன் றுற்றக்கால்
ஊராண்மை மற்றதன் எஃகு.
transliteration:
Peraanmai enba tharukan ondru utrakkaal
Ooraanmai matradhan eqku.
current_meaning: Fearlessness in battle is called great valour, but helping the enemy when misfortune strikes him is the sharp edge of that valour.
elementary_explanation: A good football player plays hard to win. But if a player on the other team falls and gets hurt, the best player stops and helps him up. Being brave is good; being brave and kind is even better.
university_explanation: This is the moral centre of the chapter: tharukan (fierceness, unflinching daring) is what people call peraanmai (great manliness or valour), but ooraanmai, helping or showing grace when ondru utrakkaal (“a calamity befalls,” understood as befalling the foe), is its eqku, the keen cutting edge. Parimelazhagar glosses ooraanmai as upakaram (benevolent aid) and the traditional reading takes the misfortune as the enemy’s, so magnanimity to a fallen foe is the sharpest point of heroism. Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar both read it this way; Sivayogi Sivakumar paraphrases more broadly as relieving others’ suffering, even enemies’. The metaphor of eqku (steel, blade-edge) is apt: valour without mercy is a blunt weapon.

tamil:
கைவேல் களிற்றொடு போக்கி வருபவன்
மெய்வேல் பறியா நகும்.
transliteration:
Kaivel kalitrodu pokki varubavan
Meyvel pariyaa nagum.
current_meaning: Having hurled his only spear at a war elephant, the hero, looking for another weapon, finds one lodged in his own body, pulls it out, and smiles.
elementary_explanation: A firefighter who has used up all the water in one hose doesn’t give up; he grabs whatever is at hand and keeps going, even laughing at how tough the day is. The warrior in this verse is like that: nothing stops him.
university_explanation: Kaivel (the spear in hand) is sent off (pokki) with the kalitru (bull elephant), and the warrior, returning weaponless (varubavan), finds a meyvel, an enemy spear stuck in his own body (mey), which he plucks out (pariyaa) and laughs (nagum). Parimelazhagar and later commentators read the laughter as joy at having found a new weapon, not as indifference to pain, so the image is about undiminished fighting spirit. Solomon Pappaiah adds that he takes the spear to hurl at the next elephant. The couplet belongs to the Sangam puram tradition of the hero who welcomes wounds, and its hyperbole should be read as a literary ideal of morale, not a literal description. The two base texts agree verbatim.

tamil:
விழித்தகண் வேல்கொண டெறிய அழித்திமைப்பின்
ஒட்டன்றோ வன்க ணவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Vizhiththakan velkonda eriya azhiththimaippin
Ottandro vankanavarkku.
current_meaning: For the truly brave, even blinking when the enemy’s spear flies toward the eyes that glare at him counts as a retreat.
elementary_explanation: A goalkeeper facing a penalty kick tries hard not to flinch, because flinching means he can’t see the ball. The verse says a brave person keeps their eyes open and steady even when something scary is coming right at them.
university_explanation: Vizhiththa kan, the wide-open, glaring eye fixed on the foe, is set against azhiththu imaippin, “if it gives way and blinks,” when the enemy hurls (eriya) his spear (vel). For the vankanavar (the hard-eyed, stout-hearted), such a blink is ottu, which commentators gloss as tantamount to puRangodai, turning one’s back in flight; Kalaignar makes this equation explicit. The couplet sets an almost impossible standard to show that heroism is first an inner state: the smallest outward sign of fear already counts as defeat. The sandhi forms கொண டெறிய = kondu eriya and வன்க ணவர்க்கு = vankanavarkku; both base sources agree.

tamil:
விழுப்புண் படாதநாள் எல்லாம் வழுக்கினுள்
வைக்கும்தன் நாளை எடுத்து.
transliteration:
Vizhuppun padaadhanaal ellaam vazhukkinul
Vaikkumdhan naalai eduththu.
current_meaning: The hero, counting up his days, sets down as wasted every day on which he received no honourable wound.
elementary_explanation: Some athletes feel a day without practice is a day wasted. The warrior here feels that way about days when he did not stand up bravely for his people. The real lesson is about not letting days slip by without doing something that matters.
university_explanation: Vizhuppun is a technical term of puram ethics: a wound of honour, received on the chest or face while facing the enemy, as opposed to a wound in the back (a sign of flight). The warrior “takes up” (eduththu) his days and places (vaikkum) every day without such a wound among vazhukku, lapses or wasted days. Solomon Pappaiah explicitly specifies wounds on face and chest, following the traditional reading. The idea echoes Purananuru poems in which a mother checks that her son’s wounds are on his chest. Modern readers may take the hyperbole as a vivid figure for a life measured by service and risk rather than comfort.

tamil:
சுழலும் இசைவேண்டி வேண்டா உயிரார்
கழல்யாப்புக் காரிகை நீர்த்து.
transliteration:
Suzhalum isaivendi vendaa uyiraar
Kazhalyaappuk kaarigai neerththu.
current_meaning: For those who seek world-encircling fame and do not cling to life, binding on the warrior’s anklet is a true adornment.
elementary_explanation: A medal looks most beautiful on someone who earned it by being brave for others. The warrior’s anklet in this verse is like that medal: it is beautiful because of the courage of the one who wears it.
university_explanation: Suzhalum isai is fame that “circles” or spreads around the world; vendaa uyiraar are those who do not desire (cling to) life; kazhal yaappu is the tying on of the kazhal, the heroic anklet worn by warriors in Tamil tradition; and kaarigai neerththu means it has the nature of a true ornament. The point is that the badge of valour is fitting only on those whose courage is real: on others it would be mere decoration. Solomon Pappaiah glosses isai as the fame that stays on earth after death, unlike the hero who departs. Both base texts agree on the wording; the sandhi யாப்புக் = yaappu + k.

tamil:
உறின்உயிர் அஞ்சா மறவர் இறைவன்
செறினும் சீர்குன்றல் இலர்.
transliteration:
Urin uyir anjaa maravar iraivan
Serinum seerkundral ilar.
current_meaning: Warriors who do not fear for their lives when war comes do not lose their fervour even if the king angrily holds them back.
elementary_explanation: A team captain may tell an eager player to sit out this game. A truly dedicated player doesn’t sulk or lose heart; they stay ready and keen. The verse says the best soldiers keep their spirit high even when told to wait.
university_explanation: Urin (“if it comes,” i.e., if battle arises) uyir anjaa maravar (warriors who do not fear for life) remain seer kundral ilar (without loss of excellence or ardour) even if iraivan serinum, “the king is angry,” which the traditional commentary reads as the king forbidding them to fight. Maravar derives from maram, martial valour, and is the classic Tamil term for the warrior class. Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan read it as the king restraining them; Kalaignar reads it as the king’s displeasure not diminishing their sense of duty. The couplet thus praises discipline without loss of spirit: zeal survives even the leader’s rebuke.

tamil:
இழைத்தது இகவாமைச் சாவாரை யாரே
பிழைத்தது ஒறுக்கிற் பவர்.
transliteration:
Izhaiththadhu igavaamaich chaavaarai yaare
Pizhaiththadhu orukkir pavar.
current_meaning: Who could blame for failure those who die keeping the vow they made?
elementary_explanation: If a friend promised to protect you and gave everything trying, no one would say they failed. Keeping your word with all your heart is what counts, even if things don’t turn out perfectly.
university_explanation: Izhaiththadhu refers to what one has pledged, the sool or battle-vow sworn before the king; igavaamai is “not transgressing” it; saavaarai are those who die so. The rhetorical question yaare ... orukkirpavar asks “who would punish (or reproach) them” for pizhaiththadhu, the failure. Commentators divide: Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it as those who die fighting in fulfilment of their vow, whom no one can reproach; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as even if the vow went unfulfilled, death in the attempt removes all blame. Either way, death in fidelity to one’s word places the warrior beyond censure.

tamil:
புரந்தார்கண் நீர்மல்கச் சாகிற்பின் சாக்காடு
இரந்துகோள் தக்கது உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Purandhaarkan neermalgach chaagirpin saakkaadu
Irandhukol thakkadhu udaiththu.
current_meaning: If a warrior can die in such a way that the eyes of the king who cared for him fill with tears, that death is worth begging for.
elementary_explanation: When someone gives everything to protect others, the people who loved and led them are deeply moved and never forget them. The verse says the greatest honour is to be so loyal and good that your leader is moved to tears for you.
university_explanation: Purandhaar are “those who nurtured or protected” the warrior, chiefly the king who maintained him; the condition is that their kan (eyes) neer malga, brim with tears; such a saakkaadu (death) has a worth that makes it irandhu kol thakkadhu, fit to be obtained even by begging (iravu, the act the Kural elsewhere treats as shameful). The paradox is deliberate: Valluvar, who devotes chapters 106-107 to the shame of begging, says this one thing is worth begging for. The couplet closes the chapter on the bond between ruler and soldier rather than on slaughter: the measure of the death is the grief of the one who knew its worth. Solomon Pappaiah renders the king’s eyes as those that weigh the heroes’ deeds; the other commentators take the tears literally.

tamil:
செயற்கரிய யாவுள நட்பின் அதுபோல்
வினைக்கரிய யாவுள காப்பு.
transliteration:
Seyarkariya yaavula natpin adhupol
vinaikkariya yaavula kaappu.
current_meaning: What is as hard to win as friendship? And once won, what guard is as hard for any hostile effort to break through?
elementary_explanation: Making a real friend is like growing a tree from a seed: it takes a long time and lots of care. But once the tree is big, it gives you shade that no storm can easily take away. A true friend is both the hardest thing to grow and the best shelter to have.
university_explanation: The chapter opens the Natpiyal (நட்பியல், section on friendship, chapters 79-95) of the Porutpal, where friendship is treated not only as a private good but as one of the supports of a king and of any householder. The couplet is built on two parallel rhetorical questions: seyaRku ariya (செயற்கரிய, hard to make or acquire) and vinaikku ariya kaappu (வினைக்கரிய காப்பு, a guard hard for hostile action to breach). Parimelazhagar reads the second line as ‘what guard is so hard for enemies’ efforts to overcome’, which is why Pope renders it ‘What so sure defence ’gainst all that foe can do?’; Mu. Varadarasanar instead takes vinai as one’s own undertakings, so that friendship is the rare protection for one’s work, and Solomon Pappaiah combines the two senses. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நிறைநீர நீரவர் கேண்மை பிறைமதிப்
பின்னீர பேதையார் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Niraineera neeravar kenmai piraimadhip
pinneera pedhaiyaar natpu.
current_meaning: Friendship with the worthy grows like the waxing crescent moon; friendship with fools shrinks like the moon after it is full.
elementary_explanation: Think of the moon. Some nights it starts as a thin smile and gets bigger and brighter every night. Other times it starts big and round and shrinks a little every night. Good friends are like the growing moon: each week you know them, the friendship gets fuller. Silly friends are like the shrinking moon: exciting at first, then less and less.
university_explanation: The couplet is one of the Kural’s best-known lunar similes. Niraineera (நிறைநீர) means ‘of the nature of filling up’, that is, the waxing crescent (piRai, பிறை) that grows to fullness; piRaimadhip pinneera (பிறைமதிப் பின்னீர) means ‘of the nature of the moon after fullness’, the waning phase. Neeravar (நீரவர்) are ‘people of good nature’ (from நீர்மை, quality), and Parimelazhagar glosses them as the wise and good, set against pēdhaiyār (பேதையார், fools). Kēṇmai and natpu are near-synonyms for friendship, used for variety. Parimelazhagar notes that the first kind of friendship starts small and grows by the day, while the second starts at its fullest and then declines. The text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நவில்தொறும் நூல்நயம் போலும் பயில்தொறும்
பண்புடை யாளர் தொடர்பு.
transliteration:
Navildhorum noolnayam polum payildhorum
panpudai yaalar thodarpu.
current_meaning: Friendship with people of fine character is like a great book: the more often you return to it, the more delight it gives.
elementary_explanation: Do you have a favourite book you have read many times? Each time, you notice something new and like it even more. Being friends with a kind, good person is like that book: every time you spend time together, the friendship gets sweeter.
university_explanation: The couplet sets two verbs of repetition side by side: navil-thoRum (நவில்தொறும், ‘each time it is studied or recited’) and payil-thoRum (பயில்தொறும், ‘each time one associates’). Nūl-nayam (நூல்நயம்) is the excellence or beauty of a learned text, which reveals new depths with every reading; paṇbudaiyāḷar (பண்புடையாளர்) are people of refined character, and thodarpu (தொடர்பு) is their companionship. Parimelazhagar’s point is that good company, unlike pleasures that tire with use, grows sweeter with each meeting, just as a good book does. The comparison fits the Kural’s own high regard for study (chapters 40-42). ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give the same text; பண்புடை யாளர் is a metrical split of பண்புடையாளர்.

tamil:
நகுதற் பொருட்டன்று நட்டல் மிகுதிக்கண்
மேற்சென்று இடித்தற் பொருட்டு.
transliteration:
Nagudhar poruttandru nattal migudhikkan
merchendru idiththar poruttu.
current_meaning: We make friends not just to laugh together, but so that when a friend goes too far, we can step in first and rebuke them.
elementary_explanation: Imagine your friend is about to cross the road without looking. A pretend friend just keeps laughing with them. A real friend grabs their arm and says, ‘Stop! That’s dangerous!’ even if it makes them a bit cross. Friends are for fun, but most of all they are for stopping each other from doing something wrong.
university_explanation: This is the chapter’s key statement on the moral purpose of friendship. Nagudhal (நகுதல்) is laughing or merriment; nattal (நட்டல்) is the act of befriending; migudhi (மிகுதி) means excess, that is, a friend’s overstepping or wrongdoing; mēRsenRu (மேற்சென்று) means ‘going ahead, taking the initiative’; and iditthal (இடித்தல், literally ‘striking’) is the classical term for sharp rebuke, related to iḍipparai (இடிப்பார், the rebuking counsellor) in kural 448. Parimelazhagar stresses that the friend must rebuke before the fault grows, without waiting to be asked. Both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print மேற்செனறு, which looks like a shared typing error; the standard reading மேற்சென்று (as in Mu. Varadarasanar’s ‘முற்பட்டுச் சென்று’ gloss) is given here.

tamil:
புணர்ச்சி பழகுதல் வேண்டா உணர்ச்சிதான்
நட்பாங் கிழமை தரும்.
transliteration:
Punarchchi pazhagudhal vendaa unarchchidhaan
natpaang kizhamai tharum.
current_meaning: Friendship does not need constant meetings or long acquaintance; a shared understanding of heart and mind is enough to give the full claim of friendship.
elementary_explanation: Sometimes you meet a pen pal or a cousin who lives far away, and even though you rarely see each other, you just ‘get’ each other. You like the same things and feel the same way. Valluvar says that feeling of understanding is what really makes a friend, not how many times you hang out.
university_explanation: PuNarchchi (புணர்ச்சி) here means being together or meeting, and pazhaguthal (பழகுதல்) long familiarity; both are declared unnecessary (vēṇdā). What creates friendship is uNarchchi (உணர்ச்சி), which Parimelazhagar glosses as like-mindedness, a mutual understanding of each other’s feelings; this alone gives natpu-ām kizhamai (நட்பாங் கிழமை), the intimate right or claim that belongs to friendship. Commentators traditionally cite the Sangam friendship of the Chola king Kōpperuñcōḻaṉ and the poet Pisirāndaiyār, who were said to have loved each other for years without meeting, and of whom the poet joined the king in his ritual fast unto death (Puranaṉūru 215-217). The text is the same on both web sources.

tamil:
முகநக நட்பது நட்பன்று நெஞ்சத்து
அகநக நட்பது நட்பு.
transliteration:
Muganaga natpadhu natpandru nenjaththu
aganaga natpadhu natpu.
current_meaning: Friendship that only makes the face smile is not friendship; friendship that makes the heart smile within is friendship.
elementary_explanation: Some people smile at you only on the outside, like a mask, but inside they don’t really care. A true friend is happy all the way inside when they see you, even if they don’t make a big show of it. Real friendship is a smile in the heart, not just on the face.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on a pair of near-rhyming compounds: muga-naga (முகநக, ‘so that the face smiles’) and aga-naga (அகநக, ‘so that the inside smiles’), with nenjatthu (நெஞ்சத்து, ‘in the heart’) making the inner sense explicit. Naga (நக) means to laugh, smile or blossom, so both commentators and translators often render it as the face or heart ‘blooming’. Parimelazhagar takes the first kind of friendship to be outward courtesy only, and the second to be friendship rooted in love (anbu). The word natpu appears four times in seven words, which gives the verse its proverbial ring. The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அழிவி னவைநீக்கி ஆறுய்த்து அழிவின்கண்
அல்லல் உழப்பதாம் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Azhivi navainikki aaruyththu azhivinkan
allal uzhappadhaam natpu.
current_meaning: Friendship turns a friend away from what would ruin him, guides him onto the right path, and, when ruin comes anyway, shares his suffering.
elementary_explanation: A real friend does three things. First, if you’re about to do something that will get you into big trouble, they stop you. Second, they help you find a better thing to do. Third, if something bad happens anyway, they don’t run away; they stay and feel sad with you. That’s what a friend is for.
university_explanation: The verse lists three duties in order: azhivinavai nīkki (அழிவினவை நீக்கி, ‘removing the things that lead to ruin’), āRu uytthu (ஆறுய்த்து, ‘sending him along the right way’, from āRu, path), and, if ruin still comes (azhivinkaN, அழிவின்கண்), allal uzhappathu (அல்லல் உழப்பது, ‘toiling in his distress alongside him’). Parimelazhagar takes the first two as prevention and correction, carrying on from the rebuke of kural 784, and the third as the friend’s readiness to share in misfortune he could not prevent. The printed line அழிவி னவைநீக்கி is a metrical split of அழிவினவை நீக்கி. Both web sources give the same text, and Pope’s ‘it weeps with him who weeps’ echoes Romans 12:15.

tamil:
உடுக்கை இழந்தவன் கைபோல ஆங்கே
இடுக்கண் களைவதாம் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Udukkai izhandhavan kaipola aange
idukkan kalaivadhaam natpu.
current_meaning: As the hand of a man whose garment slips flies at once to catch it, so friendship rushes, then and there, to remove a friend’s distress.
elementary_explanation: If your trousers started slipping in front of the whole class, your hand would grab them right away. You wouldn’t stop to think or wait to be asked; your hand just does it. A true friend helps you in trouble that fast and that naturally, as if they were your own hand.
university_explanation: This is one of the most quoted images in the Kural. Udukkai (உடுக்கை) is a garment and izhandhavan (இழந்தவன்) the one losing it, so the picture is of clothing slipping, which Solomon Pappaiah and others place ‘in front of many people’ (பலர் முன்னே) to bring out the urgency of shame. The key word is āngē (ஆங்கே, ‘there and then, at once’): the hand acts by reflex, without being asked and without thinking. Parimelazhagar notes that the hand acts before the mind decides, and so friendship should remove idukkaN (இடுக்கண், distress) before the friend has to ask. The image also implies that a friend is part of one’s own body. Both web sources give the same text.

tamil:
நட்பிற்கு வீற்றிருக்கை யாதெனின் கொட்பின்றி
ஒல்லும்வாய் ஊன்றும் நிலை.
transliteration:
Natpirku veetrirukkai yaadhenin kotpindri
ollumvaai oondrum nilai.
current_meaning: If you ask where friendship sits enthroned, it is in the steady readiness, without wavering, to hold a friend up in every way one can.
elementary_explanation: Think of a walking stick that an old person leans on. It doesn’t move around or give up; it’s always there to take their weight. Valluvar says the very best friendship is like that stick: steady, never changing its mind, and always ready to hold you up however it can.
university_explanation: VīRRirukkai (வீற்றிருக்கை) means a throne or seat of majesty, so the question is ‘where is friendship’s throne?’, that is, what is its highest state. The answer has three parts: kotpu inRi (கொட்பின்றி, ‘without kotpu’, a word meaning whirling or wavering, so ‘without change of heart’); ollum vāy (ஒல்லும்வாய், ‘wherever and however possible’); and ūnRum nilai (ஊன்றும் நிலை, ‘the state of propping up, supporting’, as a staff supports). Parimelazhagar explains ollumvāy as helping in every way available toward the friend’s virtue and wealth, and kotpinri as never wavering in mind, whatever the times. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah gloss kotpinri as ‘always, without change’. Both web sources give the same text.

tamil:
இனையர் இவரெமக்கு இன்னம்யாம் என்று
புனையினும் புல்லென்னும் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Inaiyar ivaremakku innamyaam endru
punaiyinum pullennum natpu.
current_meaning: When friends go around saying, ‘He is this much to me, and I am that much to him,’ the friendship, however finely praised, becomes cheap.
elementary_explanation: Imagine two kids who keep telling everyone, ‘I’m her best friend, and I gave her THREE presents, and she’s SO lucky to have me!’ It starts to sound like showing off, and the friendship feels less special. Real friends don’t keep score or brag about it; they just are friends.
university_explanation: Inaiyar (இனையர்) means ‘such-and-such persons’ and innam (இன்னம்) ‘such-and-such’; the friend who says ‘he is so much to us, we are so much to him’ is measuring and advertising the friendship. Punaiyinum (புனையினும், ‘even if one adorns or praises it’) and pullennum (புல்லென்னும், ‘it looks mean or paltry’, from pul, grass, a common figure for worthlessness) complete the thought. Parimelazhagar reads the couplet as a warning that true friends do not set their mutual services side by side or display their closeness, because keeping such accounts belongs to traders, not friends. The chapter thus ends where it began, by setting real friendship above any outward show. Both web sources give the same text; இவரெமக்கு is இவர் எமக்கு joined by sandhi.

tamil:
நாடாது நட்டலிற் கேடில்லை நட்டபின்
வீடில்லை நட்பாள் பவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Naadaadhu nattalir kedillai nattapin
veedillai natpaal bavarkku.
current_meaning: Nothing does more harm than making friends without first looking into a person, because for those who truly keep faith with friendship, once a friend is made there is no getting free of the bond.
elementary_explanation: Imagine tying your shoelace to a friend’s shoelace for a three-legged race. Once the knot is tight, you have to run together wherever the other person goes. So before you tie the knot, make sure your partner is someone who runs the right way.
university_explanation: The chapter opens on a paradox: the very loyalty that makes a person a good friend is what makes a careless friendship dangerous. Natpaalbavar (நட்பாள்பவர்) are ‘those who maintain friendship’, people for whom a friend once made cannot be dropped; veedu (வீடு) here means ‘release’ or ‘leaving off’, not ‘house’. Parimelazhagar draws the inference the couplet implies: since the good never abandon a friend, there is no evil equal to friendship formed without naadal (நாடல், inquiry), and so the examination must come before, not after. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it the same way, while Kalaignar paraphrases it as ‘a bad friendship taken up without inquiry brings harm one cannot escape’. The text is the same in ytamizh, thirukkural.net and the sandhi-joined edition at thirukkural-thamizh.org.

tamil:
ஆய்ந்தாய்ந்து கொள்ளாதான் கேண்மை கடைமுறை
தான்சாம் துயரம் தரும்.
transliteration:
Aaindhaaindhu kollaadhaan kenmai kadaimurai
thaansaam thuyaram tharum.
current_meaning: The friendship of someone who did not examine the other person again and again will in the end bring him grief bitter enough to kill him.
elementary_explanation: If you eat a mushroom from the woods without checking it, it might look fine today and make you very sick tomorrow. Friends are like that too. Look carefully, and then look again, before you let someone become your close friend.
university_explanation: The doubling aaindhu-aaindhu (ஆய்ந்தாய்ந்து, ‘having examined and examined’) insists that a single check is not enough; Parimelazhagar understands it as examining a person by many means and on many occasions. Kenmai (கேண்மை) is intimate friendship, and kadaimurai (கடைமுறை) means ‘at the last’ or ‘in the final course’, so the harm is delayed, which is why it is so easily ignored. Thaan saam thuyaram (தான்சாம் துயரம்) is ‘a sorrow from which he himself dies’; most modern commentators, including Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar, take this as hyperbole for grief that can bring a person to death. The sandhi-joined text at thirukkural-thamizh.org reads தான்சாந் துயரந் தரும், a purely orthographic difference from the ytamizh and thirukkural.net texts.

tamil:
குணமும் குடிமையும் குற்றமும் குன்றா
இனனும் அறிந்தியாக்க நட்பு.
transliteration:
Gunamum kudimaiyum kutramum kundraa
inanum arindhiyaakka natpu.
current_meaning: Make friends with someone only after you know his character, his family background, his faults, and the circle of people he keeps close.
elementary_explanation: Before you join a new team, you watch how the players behave, who their coach is, what mistakes they make, and who they hang out with. Valluvar says to do the same four checks before you choose a close friend.
university_explanation: This couplet supplies the checklist for the chapter’s ‘investigation’: gunam (குணம், disposition or character), kudimai (குடிமை, lineage, the family in which one is raised), kutram (குற்றம், faults), and kundraa inam (குன்றா இனம், one’s abiding associates or kin). Parimelazhagar takes inam as the circle of relatives and companions who stand by a person, on the principle, developed in chapter 46 (Sitrinam Seraamai), that a person takes on the quality of the company he keeps; Puliyur Kesigan accordingly glosses it as ‘the companions who stay with him’. Arindhu yaakka (அறிந்து யாக்க) means ‘form it having known’. The ytamizh and thirukkural.net texts read குணமும், while the sandhi-joined edition reads குணனுங் குடிமையுங், an older spelling with the same meaning.

tamil:
குடிப்பிறந்து தன்கண் பழிநாணு வானைக்
கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Kudippirandhu thankan pazhinaanu vaanaik
koduththum kolalvendum natpu.
current_meaning: Win the friendship of a person raised in a good family who is ashamed at any hint of blame, even if it costs you something to do so.
elementary_explanation: Some friends are like a good umbrella: worth saving your pocket money for. A friend who comes from a caring home and feels bad if he does something wrong is that kind of friend, so it is worth giving up something to have him.
university_explanation: Kudippirandhu (குடிப்பிறந்து) means ‘born into a good family’, the kudi of chapter 96 (Kudimai), and pazhi naanuvaan (பழிநாணுவான்) is ‘one who feels shame at blame’, that is, someone whose sense of honour keeps him from disgraceful acts. Koduththum (கொடுத்தும், ‘even by giving’) carries the force of ‘even at a price’. Parimelazhagar takes it literally as giving wealth to secure such a friend, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah likewise say ‘even by paying a price’, while Kalaignar softens it to ‘by any means’. After three couplets of warning, the chapter turns here to the positive: some friendships are worth paying for. The ytamizh and thirukkural.net texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition reads தன்கட் and கொடுத்துங் … வேண்டு, orthographic variants only.

tamil:
அழச்சொல்லி அல்லது இடித்து வழக்கறிய
வல்லார்நட்பு ஆய்ந்து கொளல்.
transliteration:
Azhachcholli alladhu idiththu vazhakkariya
vallaarnatpu aaindhu kolal.
current_meaning: Look for and keep the friendship of people who can speak hard words that make you weep, or rebuke you sharply, and who understand how the world works.
elementary_explanation: A good coach sometimes tells you, ‘That was wrong, do it again,’ and it can make you want to cry. But that coach makes you better. Valluvar says to choose friends like that coach, not friends who only say nice things.
university_explanation: Azhach cholli (அழச்சொல்லி) is ‘speaking so as to make one weep’ and idiththu (இடித்து) is ‘striking’, that is, rebuking hard; the same verb appears in kural 448 of the idikkum thunai, the counsellor who rebukes a king. Parimelazhagar distinguishes the two: the friend makes you weep with counsel before a wrong is done, and rebukes you sharply after it is done; Solomon Pappaiah follows this two-step reading. Vazhakku ariya valla (வழக்கறிய வல்ல) means ‘able to make one know the ways of the world’, adding practical wisdom to frankness. Both ytamizh and thirukkural.net print வல்லார்நடபு, which is missing its pulli; the sandhi-joined edition’s வல்லார்நட் பாய்ந்து confirms the reading வல்லார்நட்பு used here.

tamil:
கேட்டினும் உண்டோர் உறுதி கிளைஞரை
நீட்டி அளப்பதோர் கோல்.
transliteration:
Kettinum undor urudhi kilaignarai
neetti alappadhor kol.
current_meaning: Even misfortune has one benefit: it is a measuring rod that shows you, in full, how far your friends and kin really go for you.
elementary_explanation: When it rains, you find out which umbrellas have holes. When something bad happens to you, you find out which friends stay. That is the one good thing about a bad day: it shows you who your real friends are.
university_explanation: Kedu (கேடு) is ruin or misfortune and urudhi (உறுதி) is ‘benefit’ or ‘firm good’; the -um in kettinum gives ‘even in ruin’. Kilaignar (கிளைஞர்) literally means kin, ‘those of the same branch’, but Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators extend it to friends, since the chapter is about friendship. The image of neetti alappadhu oor kol (நீட்டி அளப்பதோர் கோல், ‘a rod that measures by stretching out’) is a surveyor’s measuring rod laid end to end, which measures exactly how far each person’s affection reaches. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both stress the paradox that harm itself becomes the instrument of knowledge. The sandhi-joined text reads கேட்டினு முண்டோ ருறுதி, the same words.

tamil:
ஊதியம் என்பது ஒருவற்குப் பேதையார்
கேண்மை ஒரீஇ விடல்.
transliteration:
Oodhiyam enbadhu oruvarkup pedhaiyaar
kenmai oreei vidal.
current_meaning: The real gain for a person is to give up, completely, his friendship with fools.
elementary_explanation: If your kite is tied to a heavy rock, it can never fly. Cutting the string to the rock is not a loss; it is how the kite goes up. Letting go of a friend who keeps pulling you into silly trouble is the same kind of win.
university_explanation: Oodhiyam (ஊதியம்) is ‘profit’ or ‘gain’, a deliberately commercial word in a chapter of the Porutpal. Pedhaiyaar (பேதையார்) are fools in the specific Kural sense defined in chapter 84 (Pedhaimai): people who take up what harms them and drop what helps them. Oreei (ஒரீஇ) is an alapedai (sound-lengthened) form of oruvi, ‘having abandoned’, and with vidal (விடல், ‘letting go’) it makes ‘to abandon and let go entirely’. Parimelazhagar and Puliyur Kesigan read the couplet as applying to a friendship already formed with a fool unknowingly: leaving it as soon as the folly is recognised is itself a gain. The sandhi-joined text reads ஊதிய மென்ப தொருவற்குப் … யொரீஇ, the same words.

tamil:
உள்ளற்க உள்ளம் சிறுகுவ கொள்ளற்க
அல்லற்கண் ஆற்றறுப்பார் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Ullarka ullam sirukuva kollarka
allarkan aatraruppaar natpu.
current_meaning: Do not dwell on things that shrink your spirit, and do not take up the friendship of people who will abandon you when trouble comes.
elementary_explanation: Some friends are like a bicycle that only works on sunny days: the moment it rains, the chain falls off. Do not count on a friend like that. Pick friends who will still be pedalling with you when the road gets muddy.
university_explanation: The couplet sets two prohibitions side by side. Ullarka ullam siruguva (உள்ளற்க உள்ளம் சிறுகுவ) is ‘do not think the things that make the mind small’; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take this as avoiding whatever saps one’s energy and resolve (ookkam), and Parimelazhagar treats the first line as an analogy for the second: just as one should not entertain spirit-shrinking thoughts, one should not take up such friends. Allarkan aatraruppaar (அல்லற்கண் ஆற்றறுப்பார்) are ‘those who cut off the way in time of distress’, people who withdraw their support exactly when it is needed. Puliyur Kesigan reads the first line differently, as a warning not to think meanly of a friend, which shows the line is open to more than one interpretation. The sandhi-joined text reads உள்ளற்க வுள்ளஞ் … வல்லற்க ணாற்றறுப்பார், the same words.

tamil:
கெடுங்காலைக் கைவிடுவார் கேண்மை அடுங்காலை
உள்ளினும் உள்ளஞ் சுடும்.
transliteration:
Kedungaalaik kaividuvaar kenmai adungaalai
ullinum ullanj chudum.
current_meaning: The memory of friends who abandoned you when you were falling will burn your heart, even if it comes back to you at the hour of death.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever been left alone by a friend when you really needed help? That hurt can stay with you for a very long time, even when you are grown up. Valluvar says this hurt is so strong it can burn even at the very end of life.
university_explanation: Kedungaalai (கெடுங்காலை) is ‘at the time when one is being ruined’, and adungaalai (அடுங்காலை) is ‘at the time when one is being slain’, the hour of death; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as the time when Yama comes to kill, and Kalaignar reads it as the moment one is being put to death. Ullinum (உள்ளினும், ‘even if one recalls’) and ullam sudum (உள்ளம் சுடும், ‘the heart burns’) make a play on ul- (‘think’) and ullam (‘mind’). The force of the couplet is psychological: the wound of desertion outlasts every other pain, so one should never form such a friendship in the first place, which ties it back to the chapter’s theme of investigation. The sandhi-joined text reads கேண்மை யடுங்காலை யுள்ளினு முள்ளஞ் சுடும், the same words.

tamil:
மருவுக மாசற்றார் கேண்மைஒன் றீத்தும்
ஒருவுக ஒப்பிலார் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Maruvuka maasatraar kenmaion reeththum
oruvuka oppilaar natpu.
current_meaning: Hold close the friendship of the blameless, and get out of the friendship of the unsuitable, even if you have to give something up to do it.
elementary_explanation: Think of friends like food. Keep eating the fresh fruit. If something in your lunchbox has gone bad, throw it away, even if you paid for it. Keep good friends close, and let the bad ones go even if that costs you something.
university_explanation: The closing couplet balances two imperatives in parallel: maruvuka (மருவுக, ‘cling to, embrace’) and oruvuka (ஒருவுக, ‘leave, shun’). Maasatraar (மாசற்றார்) are ‘those without stain’, while oppilaar (ஒப்பிலார்) is ambiguous: Parimelazhagar takes it as those who do not accord with the world’s good ways, Solomon Pappaiah follows with ‘those who do not fit with the world’, and Mu. Varadarasanar reads ‘those who lack matching virtue’. Onru eeththum (ஒன்று ஈத்தும், ‘even by giving something’) mirrors koduththum in kural 794: just as a good friend is worth buying, a bad one is worth paying to be rid of. The ytamizh and thirukkural.net texts read ஈத்தும், while the sandhi-joined edition divides the line as கேண்மையொன் றீத்து மொருவுக, which reads the same once the sandhi is undone.

tamil:
பழைமை எனப்படுவது யாதெனின் யாதும்
கிழமையைக் கீழ்ந்திடா நட்பு.
transliteration:
Pazhaimai enappaduvadhu yaadhenin yaadhum
kizhamaiyaik keezhndhidaa natpu.
current_meaning: If you ask what ‘long-standing friendship’ really is, it is the friendship that never slights, in any way, the liberties an old friend takes because of that closeness.
elementary_explanation: A brand-new classmate has to knock before borrowing your pencil. Your oldest friend just picks it up, and you don’t mind at all. That not-minding is what a really old friendship looks like.
university_explanation: The chapter opens with a definition. Pazhaimai (பழைமை, ‘oldness’) is the friendship that has grown old, and kizhamai (கிழமை) is the ‘right’ or ‘claim’ (urimai, உரிமை) that such long intimacy creates; keezhndhidaa (கீழ்ந்திடா) means ‘does not cut down, belittle or set aside’. Read with yaadhum (‘in anything at all’), the couplet says that true old friendship never treats the friend’s presumptions as offences. Parimelazhagar places the chapter directly after Natpaaraaydhal (testing a friend before befriending) and the commentarial tradition reads it as the next stage: once a friend has been tested and kept, the bond should bear the freedoms that time brings. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both gloss the couplet as accepting what the old friend does by right of intimacy, while Puliyur Kesigan reads it more broadly as a friendship that lets nothing damage the established bond. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நட்பிற் குறுப்புக் கெழுதகைமை மற்றதற்கு
உப்பாதல் சான்றோர் கடன்.
transliteration:
Natpir kuruppuk kezhudhakaimai matradharku
uppaadhal saandror kadan.
current_meaning: The freedoms friends take with each other are part of what friendship is made of, and it is the duty of good people to welcome those freedoms and enjoy them.
elementary_explanation: Salt makes food taste right. In a friendship, the little freedoms friends take, like finishing your sentences or grabbing a fry off your plate, are the salt. A good person does not complain about the salt; they enjoy the meal.
university_explanation: Uruppu (உறுப்பு, ‘limb, constituent part’) makes kezhudhakaimai (கெழுதகைமை, ‘the quality of intimate right’) a structural part of friendship, not an extra. The second line turns on uppu (உப்பு, ‘salt’), which the commentators read figuratively as relish or sweetness: the wise should be the salt to that intimacy, accepting it and taking pleasure in it. Mu. Varadarasanar reads uppaadhal as ‘agreeing to’ the friend’s act of right, Solomon Pappaiah as ‘rejoicing at it’, and Puliyur Kesigan as ‘acting as the very model of that intimacy’. G. U. Pope’s ‘to be its savour sweet is duty of the wise’ keeps the image of salt. Saandror (சான்றோர்) are the cultivated people whose kadan (கடன், ‘duty, obligation’) this is. Both base sources give the same text.

tamil:
பழகிய நட்பெவன் செய்யுங் கெழுதகைமை
செய்தாங்கு அமையாக் கடை.
transliteration:
Pazhakiya natpevan seyyung kezhudhakaimai
seydhaangu amaiyaak kadai.
current_meaning: What good is a friendship kept up for years if you won’t accept what your friend does by right of that closeness as though you had done it yourself?
elementary_explanation: Imagine your best friend signs both your names on a birthday card for your teacher without asking. If you get cross, what was all that friendship for? A real friend says, ‘Good idea, that’s what I would have done.’
university_explanation: The couplet is a rhetorical question: evan seyyum (எவன் செய்யும், ‘what will it do?’) asks what use a long-practised friendship (pazhakiya natpu) has if one does not seydhaangu amaidhal (செய்தாங்கு அமைதல்), ‘acquiesce as though one had done it oneself’, in what the friend did by kezhudhakaimai (intimate right). Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take this as owning the friend’s act; Solomon Pappaiah adds that this holds even when one does not personally agree with it. Puliyur Kesigan reads the line from the other side: if the same intimacy is not present in the friend too, the long acquaintance is useless. That reading shows the couplet can be taken as a statement about reciprocity. The text is the same in both base sources (with the sandhi form seyyung).

tamil:
விழைதகையான் வேண்டி இருப்பர் கெழுதகையாற்
கேளாது நட்டார் செயின்.
transliteration:
Vizhaidhakaiyaan vendi iruppar kezhudhakaiyaar
kelaadhu nattaar seyin.
current_meaning: When friends, by right of their closeness, do something without asking, the wise welcome it as something they wanted, because it came from someone they love.
elementary_explanation: Your friend sees your bike tyre is flat and pumps it up while you are at lunch, without asking. You don’t say, ‘Who gave you permission?’ You say, ‘Thanks!’ That is how old friends treat each other.
university_explanation: The key phrase is kelaadhu (கேளாது, ‘without asking’): the friend acts for us kezhudhakaiyaal, ‘by the right of intimacy’. The wise respond vizhaidhakaiyaan (விழைதகையான், ‘because of its desirability’), and vendi iruppar, ‘remain as those who wanted it’. Mu. Varadarasanar emphasises honouring the right itself, while Solomon Pappaiah says the wise accept the act even when they already knew of it, because it was done willingly by a friend. Kalaignar and Puliyur Kesigan make the same point more plainly: a good friend accepts what was done unasked. The couplet assumes a household culture in which a close friend may lawfully use or dispose of what is ours. Both base texts agree.

tamil:
பேதைமை ஒன்றோ பெருங்கிழமை என்றுணர்க
நோதக்க நட்டார் செயின்.
transliteration:
Pedhaimai ondro perungizhamai endrunarka
nodhakka nattaar seyin.
current_meaning: If a friend does something that hurts you, put it down either to simple ignorance or to the great closeness that made them feel free to do it.
elementary_explanation: If your best friend borrows your favourite book and spills juice on it, think: ‘Maybe they didn’t know it mattered so much, or maybe they just felt at home with my things.’ Don’t decide straight away that they meant to hurt you.
university_explanation: Pedhaimai (பேதைமை, ‘ignorance, folly’) and perungizhamai (பெருங்கிழமை, ‘great intimacy, strong right of friendship’) are the two charitable explanations the couplet offers for an act that is nodhakka (நோதக்க, ‘fit to cause pain’). The particle ondro (ஒன்றோ) divides the commentators. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as ‘either … or’: ignorance or intimacy. Solomon Pappaiah reads ‘not ignorance only, but also great intimacy’. Puliyur Kesigan reads it as rejecting ignorance altogether: think of it as intimacy, not ignorance. The pairing is close to Arjuna’s pramādāt praṇayena vā (‘through carelessness or through affection’) in Bhagavad Gita 11.41, a parallel worth noting even though no direct influence can be shown. The text is the same in both base sources.

tamil:
எல்லைக்கண் நின்றார் துறவார் தொலைவிடத்தும்
தொல்லைக்கண் நின்றார் தொடர்பு.
transliteration:
Ellaikkan nindraar thuravaar tholaividaththum
thollaikkan nindraar thodarpu.
current_meaning: Those who keep within the true bounds of friendship will not give up their bond with long-standing friends, even when that bond brings them loss.
elementary_explanation: Suppose your oldest friend accidentally makes your team lose the big game. A true friend doesn’t say, ‘We’re done.’ They say, ‘We’ve been friends forever, and one bad game won’t change that.’
university_explanation: The couplet balances ellai (எல்லை, ‘limit, boundary’) against tholl-ai (தொல்லை, ‘antiquity’): ellaikkan nindraar are those who stand within the limit (of friendship’s ethic), and thollaikkan nindraar are those who have stood with us from long ago. Tholaividaththum (தொலைவிடத்தும்) is read by most commentators as ‘even in loss or ruin’, from tholai- ‘to be destroyed’. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all take it as ‘even when the old friend’s acts bring harm’. Puliyur Kesigan reads it spatially, ‘even when they have gone to distant places’, and also takes thollai in its modern sense of ‘trouble’, giving ‘those who stood by us in our troubles’. The two readings change the image but keep the ethic of not abandoning old friends. Both base sources give the same text.

tamil:
அழிவந்த செய்யினும் அன்பறார் அன்பின்
வழிவந்த கேண்மை யவர்.
transliteration:
Azhivandha seyyinum anbaraar anbin
vazhivandha kenmai yavar.
current_meaning: Those whose friendship has come down a long road of love do not stop loving, even when their friends do things that bring them ruin.
elementary_explanation: Think of a very old tree with deep roots. A storm can break some branches, but the tree is still standing the next day. A friendship that has grown for years is like that: even a big hurt doesn’t pull it out of the ground.
university_explanation: Azhivandha (அழிவந்த) are ‘things that bring destruction’, and the concessive seyyinum (‘even if they do’) leads to anbaraar (அன்பறார், ‘they do not cut off love’). The subject is anbin vazhivandha kenmaiyavar, ‘those whose kenmai (கேண்மை, friendship) has come along the way of love’, which commentators take as long-standing, inherited affection. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as friendship come down ‘from of old’ (தொன்றுதொட்டு), and Solomon Pappaiah as long-standing friendship. Puliyur Kesigan alone shifts the subject, reading it as ‘our love for them will not be cut off’. The couplet is the strongest statement of the chapter’s ideal and has been criticised by modern readers as possibly encouraging tolerance of harm; the traditional commentators keep it within the framework of a tested, virtuous friendship (compare chapter 80). The text is identical in both base sources.

tamil:
கேளிழுக்கம் கேளாக் கெழுதகைமை வல்லார்க்கு
நாளிழுக்கம் நட்டார் செயின்.
transliteration:
Kelizhukkam kelaak kezhudhakaimai vallaarkku
naalizhukkam nattaar seyin.
current_meaning: For someone so secure in an intimate friendship that they won’t even listen to others talking about their friend’s faults, the day that friend actually does wrong is a day of gain, because it proves their trust.
elementary_explanation: Someone at school whispers, ‘Your best friend said something mean about you.’ You say, ‘I don’t believe it.’ Later your friend really does make a mistake, and you work it out together. Your trust was strong enough to survive both the gossip and the mistake.
university_explanation: The couplet plays on repeated sounds: kel (கேள், ‘friend, kin’) + izhukkam (இழுக்கம், ‘fault’) is ‘a friend’s fault’, and kelaa (கேளா) is ‘not listening’. Its subject is the person vallaar (வல்லார், ‘skilled, strong’) in kezhudhakaimai who refuses to hear of a friend’s faults. The difficulty is naalizhukkam (நாளிழுக்கம்). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah, following the older interpretation, take the day the friend errs as a fruitful or useful day (பயனுள்ள நாள்) for such a person. Kalaignar reverses it: if friends wrong someone of such trust, all the days of that friendship are wasted. Puliyur Kesigan reads it as the friend’s fault seeming to be merely the fault of the day. G. U. Pope (‘The day his friend offends will day of grace to him appear’) follows the first reading. The text is the same in both base sources.

tamil:
கெடாஅ வழிவந்த கேண்மையார் கேண்மை
விடாஅர் விழையும் உலகு.
transliteration:
Kedaaa vazhivandha kenmaiyaar kenmai
vidaaar vizhaiyum ulagu.
current_meaning: The world loves those who never let go of friends whose friendship has come down unbroken through the years.
elementary_explanation: People trust the kid who has had the same best friend since kindergarten. If you stick with old friends, others think, ‘I would like a friend like that too.’
university_explanation: Kedaaa (கெடாஅ) and vidaaar (விடாஅர்) carry isai-nirai alapedai, a metrical lengthening that also adds emphasis: ‘never ruined’ and ‘never letting go’. Vazhivandha kenmaiyaar are ‘those whose friendship has come down along an unbroken path’. The main verb vizhaiyum ulagu, ‘the world desires or loves’, makes loyalty to old friends a source of public esteem. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read ‘the world praises’, while Puliyur Kesigan reads ‘everyone in the world will want such a person as a friend’. Solomon Pappaiah adds the qualification ‘even if the old friend does harm’, linking this couplet to 807. The text is the same in both base sources; the sandhi-split ytamizh form keeps the alapedai spellings.

tamil:
விழையார் விழையப் படுப பழையார்கண்
பண்பின் தலைப்பிரியா தார்.
transliteration:
Vizhaiyaar vizhaiyap paduba pazhaiyaarkan
panbin thalaippiriyaa thaar.
current_meaning: Those who never fall away from their good feeling toward old friends, even when those friends err, are loved even by people who wish them ill.
elementary_explanation: There is a kid in class who is always loyal to friends, even when they mess up. Even the kids who don’t like them much have to admit, ‘Well, they’re a really good friend.’ Loyalty earns respect even from rivals.
university_explanation: Vizhaiyaar (விழையார், ‘those who do not wish one well’, i.e. enemies) becomes the agent of vizhaiyappaduba (‘are desired, loved’), a chiasmus: the unloving come to love. Pazhaiyaarkan (பழையார்கண்) is ‘toward old friends’, and panbin thalaippiriyaadhaar are ‘those who do not part from their disposition of goodwill’. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all supply ‘even though the friends do wrong’, carrying over the theme of 805-808. Puliyur Kesigan reads the reward as enemies wanting such a person as a friend. Closing the chapter with enemies’ esteem completes an arc from defining pazhaimai (801) to its social reward (809-810). Both base texts agree.

tamil:
பருகுவார் போலினும் பண்பிலார் கேண்மை
பெருகலிற் குன்றல் இனிது.
transliteration:
Parukuvaar poalinum panpilaar kenmai
perukalir kundral inidhu.
current_meaning: Even when people of poor character seem so fond of you that they could drink you in, it is sweeter for that friendship to shrink than to grow.
elementary_explanation: Some people hug you so tightly and say so many nice things that it feels wonderful. But if they are not kind or honest underneath, it is better to let that friendship get smaller instead of bigger, just like you would slowly back away from a puppy that wags its tail and also bites.
university_explanation: The chapter on tee natpu (தீ நட்பு, ‘evil friendship’) opens with its sharpest image: parukuvaar (பருகுவார்), ‘those who would drink you up’, describing a show of affection so intense it seems to swallow the friend whole. The defect is panpu-ilaar (பண்பிலார்), ‘those without good character’, so the warmth is not the test; character is. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both stress that the excess is appearance (‘தோன்றினாலும்’, ‘நடிக்கும்’), and Kalaignar speaks of being drowned in a flood of affection; all agree the right course is kundral (குன்றல்), letting the bond dwindle, rather than an abrupt break. This sets the chapter’s practical tone: Valluvar is less interested in condemning bad friends than in teaching how to reduce their hold. The text is identical in ytamizh and thirukkural.net; the sandhi-joined edition at thirukkural-thamizh.org prints ‘குன்ற லினிது’, a difference of word division only.

tamil:
உறின்நட்டு அறினொருஉம் ஒப்பிலார் கேண்மை
பெறினும் இழப்பினும் என்.
transliteration:
Urinnattu arinoruum oppilaar kenmai
perinum izhappinum en.
current_meaning: Unworthy people make friends when there is something to gain and leave when the gain is gone; whether you win or lose such friendship makes no difference.
