elementary_explanation: Imagine a classmate who sits with you only on days you bring cookies, and walks away when you don’t. Having that ‘friend’ or not having them is really the same, because they were only ever friends with the cookies.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on two paired verbs: urin nattu (உறின் நட்டு), ‘when there is gain, befriending’, and arin oruum (அறின் ஒரூஉம்), ‘when it ends, departing’; ar- here means ‘to cease or be cut off’, and oruu is the lengthened (alapedai) form of ‘leave’. The subjects are oppilaar (ஒப்பிலார்), which Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesigan take as ‘the unworthy’ or ‘those of unequal nature’, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it with a twist, ‘those who have no equal in doing this’. The closing ‘en’ (என், ‘what of it?’) is a rhetorical shrug: such friendship is neither gain nor loss. Texts differ in spelling the second word: ytamizh has ‘அறினொருஉம்’, thirukkural.net prints ‘அறின்ஙருஉம்’ (apparently a typographic slip), and the sandhi-joined edition gives ‘உறினட் டறின்னொரூஉ’; the meaning is unaffected.

tamil:
உறுவது சீர்தூக்கும் நட்பும் பெறுவது
கொள்வாரும் கள்வரும் நேர்.
transliteration:
Uruvadhu seerthookkum natpum peruvadhu
kolvaarum kalvarum ner.
current_meaning: The friend who weighs up what he stands to get, the one who loves only for the fee, and the thief are all the same kind of person.
elementary_explanation: If someone is your friend only after checking what they can get from you, they are a bit like a person who takes things without asking. A real friend doesn’t keep a price list.
university_explanation: Valluvar sets three figures in a row and declares them ner (நேர், ‘equal’): the friend who does seerthookkal (சீர்தூக்கல், ‘weighing on a balance’) of uruvadhu (உறுவது, ‘what will come to him’); those who take only peruvadhu (பெறுவது, ‘what they receive’); and kalvar (கள்வர், ‘thieves’). The middle phrase, peruvadhu kolvaar, is read by Mu. Varadarasanar, Puliyur Kesigan and Kalaignar, following the traditional gloss, as women who sell their company for payment; Solomon Pappaiah renders it as sex workers. The point is not to single anyone out but to define calculating friendship as a transaction for gain and to class it with taking what is not freely given. All three web texts agree on the wording; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘சீர்தூக்கு நட்பும்’ and ‘கள்வரு நேர்’, a matter of spelling convention.

tamil:
அமரகத்து ஆற்றறுக்கும் கல்லாமா அன்னார்
தமரின் தனிமை தலை.
transliteration:
Amarakaththu aatrarukkum kallaamaa annaar
thamarin thanimai thalai.
current_meaning: Better to be alone than to have as companions people who are like an untrained horse that throws its rider in the middle of battle.
elementary_explanation: If you ride a bike with wobbly brakes, it might fail just when you’re going downhill. A friend who leaves you at the scariest moment is like that bike, and it’s safer to walk on your own.
university_explanation: The image is martial: amarakam (அமரகம்) is ‘the battlefield’, kallaa maa (கல்லா மா) ‘a horse that has not been trained’, and aatrarukkum (ஆற்றறுக்கும்) describes it cutting the rider off midway, whether by throwing him (Mu. Varadarasanar, Kalaignar) or bolting from the field (Puliyur Kesigan, who widens maa to ‘an untaught beast’). Thamar (தமர்) means ‘one’s own people, intimates’, and the verdict is thanimai thalai (தனிமை தலை): solitude is supreme. The couplet sharpens the chapter’s logic: a bad friend is not merely useless but dangerous at exactly the moment you depend on him. The texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘அமரகத் தாற்றறுக்குங் கல்லாமா வன்னார் தமரிற் றனிமை தலை’.

tamil:
செய்தேமஞ் சாராச் சிறியவர் புன்கேண்மை
எய்தலின் எய்தாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Seydhemanj saaraach chiriyavar punkenmai
eydhalin eydhaamai nandru.
current_meaning: The shabby friendship of small-minded people, who will not stand by you as protection even when you have done everything for them, is better never gained than gained.
elementary_explanation: Think of an umbrella with holes in it. You can carry it, take care of it and open it every time, but it still won’t keep you dry. Some friends are like that, and it’s better not to count on them at all.
university_explanation: The key compound is seydhemam saaraa (செய்தேமம் சாரா): ēmam (ஏமம்) is ‘protection, safety’, and the phrase means ‘not coming to be a protection even when it has been made one’. Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as ‘though set to guard, they do not guard’, Solomon Pappaiah as ‘though we help them in many ways, they are no protection to us’, and Puliyur Kesigan as ‘they do not come to rescue us when trouble arrives’. Chiriyavar (சிறியவர்) are ‘the small’, people mean in mind, and their bond is pun-kenmai (புன்கேண்மை), ‘paltry friendship’. The conclusion, eydhalin eydhaamai nandru, ‘not attaining is better than attaining’, extends 814: such friendship is not neutral but a net loss. The text is uniform across the three sources, the sandhi-joined edition writing ‘யெய்தலி னெய்தாமை’.

tamil:
பேதை பெருங்கெழீஇ நட்பின் அறிவுடையார்
ஏதின்மை கோடி உறும்.
transliteration:
Pedhai perungezheei natpin arivudaiyaar
edhinmai kodi urum.
current_meaning: Being a stranger, or even an opponent, to wise people is worth ten million times more than the closest friendship with a fool.
elementary_explanation: If you’re building a sandcastle, a careful kid who doesn’t like you will still not knock it over, but a clumsy best friend might jump right on it while trying to help. Sometimes a sensible rival is safer than a silly friend.
university_explanation: The couplet sets pedhai perung kezheei natpu (பேதை பெருங்கெழீஇ நட்பு), ‘the greatly intimate friendship of a fool’, against arivudaiyaar edhinmai (அறிவுடையார் ஏதின்மை), and the reading of edhinmai divides commentators. Edhilaar means ‘strangers, outsiders’, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesigan take edhinmai as ‘the absence of friendship’, being unconnected to the wise; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar sharpen it to ‘enmity’ (பகை), giving the more striking proverb ‘a wise enemy is better than a foolish friend’. Kezheei (கெழீஇ) is the alapedai form of kezhu-, ‘to be closely joined’. ‘Kodi urum’ (கோடி உறும்) means ‘is worth a crore’, i.e., ten million times over. The texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘நட்பி னறிவுடையா ரேதின்மை’.

tamil:
நகைவகைய ராகிய நட்பின் பகைவரால்
பத்தடுத்த கோடி உறும்.
transliteration:
Nakaivakaiya raakiya natpin pakaivaraal
paththaduththa kodi urum.
current_meaning: What comes to you from your enemies is worth a hundred million times more than the friendship of people who only laugh along with you.
elementary_explanation: A friend who just giggles at everything never tells you there’s spinach in your teeth. Even someone who doesn’t like you might point it out. Sometimes honest criticism helps more than easy laughter.
university_explanation: Nakaivakaiyar (நகைவகையர்) are ‘those of the laughing kind’: Mu. Varadarasanar adds ‘laughing outwardly without love within’, Kalaignar ‘those who laugh and talk as a performance’, and Puliyur Kesigan ‘those useful only for idle talk and merriment’. Against them stands what comes from pakaivar (பகைவர், ‘enemies’), worth paththaduththa kodi (பத்தடுத்த கோடி), ‘ten crore’ or a hundred million times more. The exaggeration escalates the kodi of 816. Commentators differ on what an enemy provides: most modern glosses say ‘benefit’, while Kalaignar paradoxically says even the suffering enemies cause is worth more, because it at least makes one alert. The wording agrees across ytamizh and thirukkural.net; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘நட்பிற் பகைவராற்’.

tamil:
ஒல்லும் கருமம் உடற்று பவர்கேண்மை
சொல்லாடார் சோர விடல்.
transliteration:
Ollum karumam udatru pavarkenmai
sollaadaar sora vidal.
current_meaning: With those who spoil a task that could easily be done, pretending they cannot help, let the friendship quietly slacken without making an announcement of it.
elementary_explanation: If a friend always says ‘I can’t’ whenever you need a small hand, even when they easily could, you don’t need to have a big fight. You can just slowly spend more time with friends who do help.
university_explanation: Ollum karumam (ஒல்லும் கருமம்) is ‘a task that can be done’; udatrupavar (உடற்றுபவர்) are those who ‘harass’ or ruin it, which Solomon Pappaiah and the classical English versions read as feigning inability to do what they could, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar as making the possible impossible. The remedy is notably mild: sollaadaar (சொல்லாடார்), ‘without speaking of it’, sora vidal (சோர விடல்), ‘let it slacken’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read sollaadaar as ‘without letting them know’, Puliyur Kesigan as ‘by ceasing to talk with them’. The counsel is gradual disengagement rather than confrontation, a tactful way to avoid making a fresh enemy. The texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘ஒல்லுங் கரும முடற்று பவர்கேண்மை’.

tamil:
கனவினும் இன்னாது மன்னோ வினைவேறு
சொல்வேறு பட்டார் தொடர்பு.
transliteration:
Kanavinum innaadhu manno vinaiveru
solveru pattaar thodarpu.
current_meaning: Friendship with people whose deeds are one thing and whose words another is painful even in a dream.
elementary_explanation: If a friend promises to save you a seat and then gives it to someone else, and does it again and again, you start feeling uneasy even when you’re just thinking about them. A friend’s words and actions should match.
university_explanation: The couplet names the fault precisely: vinai veru, sol veru (வினை வேறு, சொல் வேறு), ‘deed apart, word apart’, the divorce of action from speech. Kanavinum (கனவினும், ‘even in a dream’) intensifies: such a connection hurts not only in waking life, as Puliyur Kesigan spells out, but even in sleep. Manno (மன்னோ) is an emotive particle of emphasis or lament, which Sivayogi Sivakumar renders as a rhetorical question, ‘will it not give pain even in a dream?’ The word here is thodarpu (தொடர்பு, ‘connection, association’) rather than natpu, perhaps suggesting such people never achieve true friendship. All three texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition prints ‘கனவினு மின்னாது’.

tamil:
எனைத்தும் குறுகுதல் ஓம்பல் மனைக்கெழீஇ
மன்றில் பழிப்பார் தொடர்பு.
transliteration:
Enaiththum kurukudhal ombal manaikkezheei
mandril pazhippaar thodarpu.
current_meaning: Guard against coming even slightly close to people who are friendly with you at home but run you down in public.
elementary_explanation: Imagine someone who plays nicely with you at your house but makes fun of you in front of the whole class. That’s not a real friend, and it’s wise to keep your distance from them.
university_explanation: The chapter closes on the double-faced friend: manaik kezheei (மனைக் கெழீஇ), ‘intimate in the house’, and mandril pazhippaar (மன்றில் பழிப்பார்), ‘those who revile in the manram’, the public hall or assembly where reputations are made. The prescription is the strongest in the chapter: enaiththum kurukudhal ombal (எனைத்தும் குறுகுதல் ஓம்பல்), ‘guard against approaching in any measure at all’. Where 811 and 818 allowed a gradual waning, here even the slightest contact is to be avoided, since such a person turns private trust into public damage. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesigan all read manai literally as ‘home’, while Kalaignar’s gloss refers to private moments. The texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition writes ‘எனைத்துங் குறுகுத லோம்பன்’ and ‘மன்றிற் பழிப்பார்’.

tamil:
சீரிடம் காணின் எறிதற்குப் பட்டடை
நேரா நிரந்தவர் நட்பு.
transliteration:
Seeridam kaanin erithar̲kup pattadai
neraa niranthavar natpu.
current_meaning: The friendship of people who keep company with you without being one with you in heart is like an anvil: it seems to hold you up, but it is really the base on which you will be struck down once they find the right moment.
elementary_explanation: A blacksmith’s anvil looks like a strong, steady table, but its real job is to hold the metal still so the hammer can hit it. A fake friend can feel like solid support, but they are only holding you in place until it suits them to let you get hurt.
university_explanation: The chapter title kooḍaa naṭpu (கூடா நட்பு) means ‘friendship that does not truly join’, and this opening couplet defines it: those who are neraa (நேரா, not inwardly agreeing) yet niranthavar (நிரந்தவர், outwardly close). Paṭṭaḍai (பட்டடை) is the smith’s anvil, the block on which metal is laid to be cut; Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read the simile this way, Pappaiah adding that it looks like support while really serving the cutting. Seer-idam (சீரிடம்) is ‘the fitting place or occasion’, so the danger lies in timing: the false friend waits for an opening. Parimelazhagar places this chapter after Thee Natpu (82, evil friendship) as a treatment of friendship that is enmity in disguise, a theme he reads in a royal-political frame. The couplet is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இனம்போன்று இனமல்லார் கேண்மை மகளிர்
மனம்போல வேறு படும்.
transliteration:
Inampondru inamallaar kenmai magalir
manampola veru padum.
current_meaning: The friendship of those who act like your own people but are not, will shift and change according to what they can gain, never holding one steady form.
elementary_explanation: Some kids are your friend only when you have the best snack at lunch. The day you have nothing to share, they sit somewhere else. Their friendship changes shape depending on what they can get.
university_explanation: Inam (இனம்) means one’s own circle or kin; inam-pondru inam-allaar are those who resemble kin but are not. Kenmai (கேண்மை) is intimacy or friendship. The comparison with magalir manam (மகளிர் மனம்) is read by Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators (Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar, Puliyur Kesigan) specifically as the mind of courtesans (பொதுமகளிர் / விலைமகளிர்), whose affection follows payment, not as a judgment on women in general; Puliyur Kesigan glosses the point as changing ‘according to the gain received’. The comparison reflects the social assumptions of its age, but its logical point is clear: an attachment driven by gain changes when the gain changes. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பலநல்ல கற்றக் கடைத்து மனநல்லர்
ஆகுதல் மாணார்க் கரிது.
transliteration:
Palanalla kat̲rak kadaiththu mananallar
aaguthal maanaark karithu.
current_meaning: Even after they have studied many good books, it is hard for people who lack inner nobility to become truly good-hearted toward you.
elementary_explanation: You can read every book about kindness and still be unkind. Knowing the rules of a game does not make you a fair player. A person who doesn’t care about you can learn lots of nice words without their heart changing.
university_explanation: Pala nalla katrak kadaiththu (பலநல்ல கற்றக் கடைத்து) means ‘even when it happens that they have learned many good things’; mana-nallar (மனநல்லர்) are the good-hearted. Maanaar (மாணார்) literally means ‘those who are not excellent’; Varadarasanar glosses it as those who have not attained greatness through inner affection, while Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as those hostile at heart (பகையுணர்வு படைத்தோர்), and Pope’s gloss ‘enemies’ follows the latter. The couplet thus warns against assuming that a learned enemy has been softened by learning: knowledge of virtue is not virtue. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா
வஞ்சரை அஞ்சப் படும்.
transliteration:
Mugaththin iniya nagaaa agaththinnaa
vanjarai anjap padum.
current_meaning: Be wary of deceivers who smile sweetly with their faces while their hearts are bitter toward you.
elementary_explanation: A shiny red apple can still have a worm inside. A big smile on the outside does not always mean kindness on the inside, so it is wise to watch what people do, not just how they smile.
university_explanation: The couplet sets mugam (முகம், face) against agam (அகம், the inner self), a pairing that will return in Kural 830. Nagaaa (நகாஅ, ‘smiling’) shows alapeḍai, the metrical lengthening of a vowel, and akaththinnaa (அகத்து இன்னா) means ‘bitter or harmful within’. Vanjar (வஞ்சர்) are deceivers, and anjappaḍum (அஞ்சப்படும்) is the impersonal ‘is to be feared’; Varadarasanar reads it as fearing to make friends with them, Kalaignar as fearing them and keeping away. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மனத்தின் அமையா தவரை எனைத்தொன்றும்
சொல்லினால் தேறற்பாற்று அன்று.
transliteration:
Manaththin amaiyaa thavarai enaiththondrum
sollinaal ther̲ar̲paat̲ru andru.
current_meaning: In no matter whatever should you rely on the words of people who are not one with you in heart.
elementary_explanation: If someone keeps promising to share their toys but never does, you learn to stop believing the promise. Words are easy to say. When someone does not really care about you, what they say is not something to lean on.
university_explanation: Manaththin amaiyaathavar (மனத்தின் அமையாதவர்) are ‘those not settled with us in mind’; enaiththondrum (எனைத்தொன்றும்) means ‘in anything at all’. Theraṟpaaṯru anru (தேறற்பாற்று அன்று) means ‘it is not fit to be trusted or relied upon’, using theṟal (தேறல், clear conviction), the same root as the chapter Therindhu Thelidhal (51) on testing before trusting. Varadarasanar reads it as not trusting their words in any undertaking, and Kalaignar as not being able to reach any clear decision on such people’s words. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நட்டார்போல் நல்லவை சொல்லினும் ஒட்டார்சொல்
ஒல்லை உணரப் படும்.
transliteration:
Nattaarpol nallavai sollinum ottaarsol
ollai unarap padum.
current_meaning: Even when enemies say good things as if they were friends, the real nature of their words is soon seen through.
elementary_explanation: A wolf can try to sound like a sheep, but sooner or later it growls. When someone who doesn’t like you starts talking sweetly, listen carefully; the truth usually shows up quickly.
university_explanation: Naṭṭaar (நட்டார்) are friends, those who have made friendship, and oṭṭaar (ஒட்டார்) are those who do not ‘stick’ or join with us, that is, foes. Nallavai sollinum (நல்லவை சொல்லினும்) concedes that the words themselves may be good, and ollai (ஒல்லை) means ‘quickly’. The couplet is partly reassurance: false friendship tends to betray itself in speech, and Kalaignar says the meanness in such words will come out without fail. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read the ‘understanding’ as recognising quickly that the words are not truly meant for our good. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
சொல்வணக்கம் ஒன்னார்கண் கொள்ளற்க வில்வணக்கம்
தீங்கு குறித்தமை யான்.
transliteration:
Solvanakkam onnaarkan kollar̲ka vilvanakkam
theengu kur̲iththamai yaan.
current_meaning: Do not take a foe’s humble, bowing speech at face value: a bow bends low only in order to do harm.
elementary_explanation: When an archer pulls back a bow, it bends down low, almost like it is bowing politely. But that bend is what sends the arrow flying. Sometimes people who don’t like you act extra polite right before they try to hurt you.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on a pun in vaṇakkam (வணக்கம்), which means both ‘bowing, reverence’ and ‘bending’: sol-vaṇakkam is ‘humility in speech’, vil-vaṇakkam ‘the bending of a bow’. Onnaar (ஒன்னார்) are those who are not one with us, enemies. Since the bow’s bend ‘signals harm’ (theengu kuṟiththamaiyaan, தீங்கு குறித்தமையான்), a foe’s deferential words should be read the same way; Pappaiah and Kalaignar draw out the simile in this sense, and Pope translates ‘pliant speech’ and ‘pliant bow’. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
தொழுதகை யுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும் ஒன்னார்
அழுதகண் ணீரும் அனைத்து.
transliteration:
Thozhuthagai yullum padaiyodungum onnaar
azhuthagan neerum anaiththu.
current_meaning: A weapon may lie hidden even in the hands that foes join in worship toward you, and the tears they shed are of the same kind.
elementary_explanation: Imagine someone bowing to you with hands pressed together, but hiding a water balloon behind them. Pretend sadness can be a trick too. If someone has been mean to you, a show of respect or tears doesn’t always mean they have changed.
university_explanation: Thozhuthagai (தொழுதகை) is the hand joined in worship or salutation, and paḍai oḍungum (படை ஒடுங்கும்) means ‘a weapon lies concealed’. The second line extends the image: onnaar azhutha kaṇṇeer (ஒன்னார் அழுத கண்ணீர், the tears foes have wept) is anaiththu (அனைத்து, of that same kind). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read the couplet literally as a weapon concealed in the worshipping hand, and Kalaignar adds that even in weeping their hearts are full of plotting. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; thirukkural.net prints the words as தொழுதகை யுள்ளும் and கண் ணீரும் with the same metrical division.

tamil:
மிகச்செய்து தம்மெள்ளு வாரை நகச்செய்து
நட்பினுள் சாப்புல்லற் பாற்று.
transliteration:
Migachcheythu thammellu vaarai nagachcheythu
natpinul saappullar̲ paat̲ru.
current_meaning: Those who make a great show of friendship while secretly despising you should be kept smiling on the surface, while you let that friendship die within yourself.
elementary_explanation: If a classmate is super-friendly to your face but laughs at you behind your back, you don’t have to start a fight. You can stay polite and friendly when you meet, but quietly stop trusting them and stop sharing your secrets.
university_explanation: Migachcheythu (மிகச்செய்து) is ‘making much of (friendship)’, and thammeḷḷuvaar (தம் எள்ளுவார்) are ‘those who scorn us’ within. The difficult phrase saappullaṟpaaṯru (சாப்புல்லற்பாற்று) is read by the commentators as ‘one should embrace (pullal) in such a way that it dies (saa)’: Varadarasanar says one should make them laugh in that friendship while acting so that the bond dies, and Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as answering pretence with pretence. Pope’s explanation, in the tradition of Parimelazhagar’s royal-political reading, presents this as the duty of kings toward such foes. Whether read as defensive policy or as cynicism, the couplet assumes a political setting where open rupture is costly; ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give identical text.

tamil:
பகைநட்பாம் காலம் வருங்கால் முகநட்டு
அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ விடல்.
transliteration:
Paganatpaam kaalam varungaal muganattu
aganatpu oreei vidal.
current_meaning: When the time comes that an enemy must be treated as a friend, be friendly in face, but keep friendship out of your heart, and let it go when you can.
elementary_explanation: Sometimes you have to work on a group project with someone who has been unkind to you. You can be polite and work together, but you don’t have to hand them your diary. Be friendly on the outside and careful on the inside.
university_explanation: Pagai-naṭpaam kaalam (பகை நட்பாம் காலம்) is ‘a time when enmity turns into friendship’, for instance an alliance forced by circumstances. The couplet resolves the chapter with the face/heart pair already used in Kural 824: muga-naṭṭu (முகநட்டு, befriending with the face) but aga-naṭpu oreei (அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ, removing friendship from the heart). Oreei (ஒரீஇ) is the alapeḍai-lengthened form of oree, ‘leaving’, and viḍal (விடல்) means ‘one should give it up’. Varadarasanar reads the final word as giving up even the outward friendship when the chance comes, Pappaiah as letting go of it in the mind, and Pope follows the first reading with ‘give up (even the former)’. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பேதைமை என்பதொன்று யாதெனின் ஏதங்கொண்டு
ஊதியம் போக விடல்.
transliteration:
Pedhaimai enbadhondru yaadhenin edhangkondu
oodhiyam poga vidal.
current_meaning: If you ask what folly is, it is this: grabbing hold of what harms you and letting what would profit you slip away.
elementary_explanation: Imagine someone offers you a choice between a shiny toy that will break in a day and a bicycle you could ride for years, and you pick the toy and walk away from the bike. That swap, keeping the bad thing and dropping the good one, is exactly what the poet calls being foolish.
university_explanation: Valluvar opens the chapter with a definition rather than an example: pedhaimai (பேதைமை) is the act of taking up edham (ஏதம், harm, loss) and letting oodhiyam (ஊதியம், gain, profit) go. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read the pair as a ledger of consequences: the fool does not merely fail to gain, he actively trades gain for loss, which is why folly is placed in the Natpiyal section right after the chapters on bad friendship. Puliyur Kesigan sharpens this into a cost-benefit reading (accepting the trouble that comes with a task while throwing away the profit it would bring), whereas Sivayogi Sivakumar reads edhangkondu as ‘out of fear of a small hardship’, a softer psychological gloss. Kalaignar stresses the failure of discernment: the fool never clarifies which is harmful and which is beneficial. The text is identical in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பேதைமையுள் எல்லாம் பேதைமை காதன்மை
கையல்ல தன்கட் செயல்.
transliteration:
Pedhaimaiyul ellaam pedhaimai kaadhanmai
kaiyalla thankat seyal.
current_meaning: The worst folly of all is to set one’s heart on deeds that are not fitting for oneself.
elementary_explanation: A goldfish might dream of climbing trees like a squirrel, but if it jumps out of its bowl to try, it will only get hurt. The silliest mistake is wanting badly to do things that are not right for who you are.
university_explanation: The couplet ranks follies and puts at the top kaadhanmai (காதன்மை, fond desire, love) for kaiyalla (கையல்ல, what is not within one’s proper hand or conduct). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar take kaiyalla as acts unsuited to one’s own moral conduct (ஒழுக்கம்), which matches G. U. Pope’s ‘deeds which to your station unbefitting prove’ and Drew’s ‘delight in doing what is forbidden’. Kalaignar instead reads it as deeds beyond one’s ability, Solomon Pappaiah as desiring things that do one no good, and Puliyur Kesigan as both choosing an undesirable act and doing it unfittingly; the line thus spans a moral reading (forbidden) and a prudential one (beyond one’s scope). The wording is the same in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நாணாமை நாடாமை நாரின்மை யாதொன்றும்
பேணாமை பேதை தொழில்.
transliteration:
Naanaamai naadaamai naarinmai yaadhondrum
penaamai pedhai thozhil.
current_meaning: Feeling no shame at wrong, not seeking what is worth seeking, having no affection, and caring for nothing at all: these are the habits of the fool.
elementary_explanation: Think of a kid who breaks a window and doesn’t feel sorry, never tries to learn anything, isn’t kind to friends, and leaves their toys out in the rain. Each of those things on its own is a warning sign; together they are what the poet calls a fool.
university_explanation: The couplet is a fourfold catalogue built on negative nouns ending in -aamai/-inmai: naanaamai (நாணாமை, shamelessness at what deserves shame), naadaamai (நாடாமை, not seeking out what deserves seeking), naarinmai (நாரின்மை, lack of naar, ‘fibre’, a metaphor for the affection that binds people), and penaamai (பேணாமை, not cherishing or protecting anything). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar gloss naar as anbu (love), and the commentators agree the list describes a whole disposition rather than isolated faults; Pope renders it ‘Ashamed of nothing, searching nothing out, of loveless heart, / Nought cherishing’. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads naarinmai as lacking sweetness of manner, a minor variation. The text is identical in both base sources.

tamil:
ஓதி உணர்ந்தும் பிறர்க்குரைத்தும் தானடங்காப்
பேதையின் பேதையார் இல்.
transliteration:
Odhi unarndhum pirarkkuraiththum thaanadangaap
pedhaiyin pedhaiyaar il.
current_meaning: No fool is greater than the one who has studied, understood, and even taught others, yet does not himself live by what he learned.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a swimming coach who teaches everyone how to stay safe in the pool but then jumps into the deep end without looking. Knowing the rules and telling others is not enough; the biggest silliness is not following them yourself.
university_explanation: The couplet climbs three steps, odhi (ஓதி, having recited or studied), unarndhum (உணர்ந்தும், having understood) and pirarkku uraiththum (பிறர்க்கு உரைத்தும், having explained to others), and then collapses on thaan adangaa (தான் அடங்கா, himself not restrained, not conforming). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar take adangudhal as living within the discipline the texts teach, and the superlative pedhaiyin pedhaiyaar il (‘there is no fool beyond this fool’) makes the learned hypocrite the extreme case of the chapter. Puliyur Kesigan glosses adangaa as lacking self-restraint (adakkam), linking the couplet to the chapter on Adakkamudaimai. All four commentaries and the two base texts agree on the reading.

tamil:
ஒருமைச் செயலாற்றும் பேதை எழுமையும்
தான்புக் கழுந்தும் அளறு.
transliteration:
Orumaich cheyalaatrum pedhai ezhumaiyum
thaanpuk kazhundhum alaru.
current_meaning: In a single lifetime the fool can bring about the hell into which he will sink through all seven births to come.
elementary_explanation: A few minutes of scribbling with permanent marker on your bedroom wall can leave a mess that takes weeks to clean. The poet says the foolish person can make, in one life, a mess so big it sticks to him for a very long time.
university_explanation: The couplet sets orumai (ஒருமை, one birth) against ezhumai (எழுமை, the seven births), and alaru (அளறு, literally ‘mire’ or ‘mud’) is the traditional word for naragam, hell. Parimelazhagar, Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah all read it eschatologically: in one life the fool is able to make (ஆற்றும்) the hell he will enter and sink into across seven births. Kalaignar departs from this, reading orumaich cheyal as ‘self-willed action’ and alaru as a mire of suffering in this world, a deliberately non-theological gloss; Puliyur Kesigan’s note on thirukkural.net is truncated. Pope’s ‘The fool will merit hell in one brief life on earth’ follows the traditional reading. The text is the same in both base sources.

tamil:
பொய்படும் ஒன்றோ புனைபூணும் கையறியாப்
பேதை வினைமேற் கொளின்.
transliteration:
Poipadum ondro punaipoonum kaiyariyaap
pedhai vinaimer kolin.
current_meaning: When a fool who does not know how to do a thing takes on a task, the work fails, and not only that: he ends up putting himself in chains.
elementary_explanation: If someone who has never cooked tries to make a big dinner alone, the food gets burnt, and they might also burn their hand. Taking on a job you don’t know how to do can spoil the job and hurt you too.
university_explanation: Kaiyariyaa (கையறியா) means ‘not knowing the method’ (kai here is the way of doing), and the couplet’s rhetorical ondro (ஒன்றோ, ‘is it only one thing?’) introduces a double penalty: the work poipadum (பொய்படும், comes to nothing) and the doer punai poonum (புனைபூணும், wears fetters). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesigan take punai literally as the shackles of a man held culpable, which Pope follows (‘himself he binds with chains’), while Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar soften it to ‘he too is ruined’ or ‘punishes himself’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss kaiyariyaa morally (not knowing the right way of conduct), whereas Pappaiah reads it practically (not knowing how to do the work). Both base sources give the same text.

tamil:
ஏதிலார் ஆரத் தமர்பசிப்பர் பேதை
பெருஞ்செல்வம் உற்றக் கடை.
transliteration:
Edhilaar aarath thamarpasippar pedhai
perunjelvam utrak kadai.
current_meaning: When a fool comes into great wealth, strangers feast on it while his own people go hungry.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a boy who wins a huge bag of candy and hands it all out to kids he barely knows, while his little sister at home gets none. Having lots of something doesn’t help your family if you don’t know how to share it wisely.
university_explanation: The couplet contrasts edhilaar (ஏதிலார், strangers, those with no tie) who aara (ஆர, eat their fill) with thamar (தமர், one’s own kin) who pasippar (பசிப்பர், go hungry). Puliyur Kesigan follows the traditional explanation that the fool’s wealth comes from past merit (munvinai), while the lack of judgment in spending it is his own; Parimelazhagar’s tradition reads the strangers as flatterers and parasites who gather round new wealth. Kalaignar’s gloss stresses that outsiders ‘roll up’ the money while affectionate kin go without. Pope renders edhilaar as ‘foes’, a stronger word than the Tamil requires; Drew’s ‘neighbours’ is closer. The text is the same in both base sources.

tamil:
மையல் ஒருவன் களித்தற்றால் பேதைதன்
கையொன்று உடைமை பெறின்.
transliteration:
Maiyal oruvan kaliththatraal pedhaidhan
kaiyondru udaimai perin.
current_meaning: When a fool gets something into his hands, it is like a man already out of his mind who has also become drunk.
elementary_explanation: Picture a kid who is already running wild at a party and then gets a big bag of sugar. Things go from silly to much worse! Giving power or money to someone who doesn’t think clearly only makes their foolishness bigger.
university_explanation: The simile doubles the condition: maiyal (மையல், bewilderment, madness) is a man already deranged, and kaliththal (களித்தல்) is intoxication by toddy, so the fool who gains udaimai (உடைமை, possession) is a madman who is also drunk. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both gloss maiyal as piththu (பித்து, madness) and kaliththal as being dazed by kal (கள், toddy), and Puliyur Kesigan adds that such a man drinks more and more and strays from his course. Kai ondru (கை ஒன்று) is read as ‘anything in his hand’, so the point holds for any wealth or authority, not only great fortune. Pope (‘as when a mad man raves in drunken glee’) and Drew follow the same reading, and the two base sources agree on the text.

tamil:
பெரிதினிது பேதையார் கேண்மை பிரிவின்கண்
பீழை தருவதொன் றில்.
transliteration:
Peridhinidhu pedhaiyaar kenmai pirivinkan
peezhai tharuvadhon ril.
current_meaning: Friendship with fools is very sweet indeed, for when it ends, there is nothing in the parting that causes any pain.
elementary_explanation: Some friends are like a balloon on a string: it is fun for a while, but when it floats away you don’t really miss it. The poet is joking that friends who are foolish are ‘lovely’, because losing them doesn’t hurt at all.
university_explanation: The couplet is ironic praise: peridhu inidhu (பெரிது இனிது, ‘exceedingly sweet’) is applied to pedhaiyaar kenmai (பேதையார் கேண்மை, friendship with fools), and the reason given is that at pirivu (பிரிவு, separation) there is no peezhai (பீழை, pain, affliction). Mu. Varadarasanar, Kalaignar and Puliyur Kesigan all read it as saying that a fool’s friendship is ‘sweet’ only in that losing it costs nothing, so its real worth is zero; Kesigan hedges with ‘in one way’. Solomon Pappaiah reads it slightly differently, as friendship among fools themselves, whose partings cause them no grief, which matches Drew’s ‘the friendship between fools’. The text is the same in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கழாஅக்கால் பள்ளியுள் வைத்தற்றால் சான்றோர்
குழாஅத்துப் பேதை புகல்.
transliteration:
Kazhaaakkaal palliyul vaiththatraal saandror
kuzhaaaththup pedhai pugal.
current_meaning: A fool entering an assembly of the wise is like putting unwashed feet on a clean bed.
elementary_explanation: Imagine coming in from a muddy football field and climbing straight into a freshly made bed with dirty feet. Everything gets messy. The poet says a fool barging into a group of wise people spoils things in the same way.
university_explanation: The closing simile sets kazhaaak kaal (கழாஅக்கால், unwashed foot) in palli (பள்ளி) against the fool’s pugal (புகல், entering) into saandror kuzhaaam (சான்றோர் குழாஅம், the gathering of the noble). The lengthened forms kazhaaa- and kuzhaaa- are isai-nirai alapedai (இசைநிறை அளபெடை), vowel prolongation that fills out the metre. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take palli as a bed (as do Pope and Drew), but Puliyur Kesigan reads it as a place of worship (‘தொழுகைக்குரிய பள்ளி’), making the image one of defiling a sanctuary; both senses of palli are attested in Tamil. The text is identical in both base sources.

tamil:
அறிவின்மை இன்மையுள் இன்மை பிறிதின்மை
இன்மையா வையா துலகு.
transliteration:
Arivinmai inmaiyul inmai piridhinmai
inmaiyaa vaiyaa thulagu.
current_meaning: Of all the kinds of lack, the lack of understanding is the real poverty; the world does not count the lack of other things, such as money, as true want.
elementary_explanation: Imagine two kids: one has an empty piggy bank but knows how to read, count and solve problems; the other has a full piggy bank but can’t figure anything out. The first one can earn coins again, but the second one will keep losing them. That is why the poet says not knowing is the emptiest pocket of all.
university_explanation: The chapter opens with a paradox built on the repeated word inmai (இன்மை, lack, poverty): arivinmai (அறிவின்மை, absence of understanding) is ‘the poverty among poverties’, while piridhinmai (other lacks, chiefly of wealth) the world will not reckon as poverty at all. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar render it as ‘the famine of knowledge is the cruelest famine’, and Solomon Pappaiah shifts the evaluator from ‘the world’ (ulagu) to ‘the great ones’ (periyor), reflecting the classical commentary habit of reading ulagu as ‘the wise of the world’. Puliyur Kesigan adds that material poverty is not regarded as lasting poverty, since it can be remedied, whereas folly cannot. Placed in the Natpiyal after Pedhaimai (ch. 84), Pullarivaanmai shifts the focus from simple folly to the conceited, perverse ignorance (pull-arivu, ‘petty knowledge’) of one who thinks himself wise. Text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the second line is printed in its traditional sandhi-split form ‘inmaiyaa vaiyaa thulagu’ (for vaiyaadhu ulagu).

tamil:
அறிவிலான் நெஞ்சுவந்து ஈதல் பிறிதியாதும்
இல்லை பெறுவான் தவம்.
transliteration:
Arivilaan nenjuvandhu eedhal piridhiyaadhum
illai peruvaan thavam.
current_meaning: When a fool gives something away with a glad heart, the cause is nothing else but the good merit of the one who receives it.
elementary_explanation: Suppose a kid who never shares suddenly hands you his best sandwich with a big smile. You didn’t earn it from his good sense; you were just lucky that day. The poet says a fool’s gift is like that: it comes from the receiver’s good luck, not the giver’s wisdom.
university_explanation: The kural is ironic: a person without understanding (arivilaan, அறிவிலான்) does not give wisely, so if he gives nenjuvandhu (நெஞ்சுவந்து, with a gladdened heart), the explanation must lie outside him, in the thavam (தவம், austerity, accumulated merit) of the recipient (peruvaan). Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah gloss thavam as nalvinai (good karma), and the old English rendering speaks of ‘the receiver’s merit (in a former birth)’, reflecting the karmic reading of the classical commentators. Kalaignar softens it to ‘the receiver’s good fortune’, while Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as the receiver’s own spiritual quality drawing the gift. The underlying point is that the fool’s generosity is unreliable and unearned, an accident of providence rather than a virtue. No textual variants appear between ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அறிவிலார் தாந்தம்மைப் பீழிக்கும் பீழை
செறுவார்க்கும் செய்தல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Arivilaar thaandhammaip peezhikkum peezhai
seruvaarkkum seydhal aridhu.
current_meaning: The suffering fools bring upon themselves is greater than anything even their enemies could manage to inflict on them.
elementary_explanation: Think of a kid who won’t wear a coat in the snow, eats all the candy at once and then skips homework. No bully could make his day as miserable as he has made it himself. The poet says fools are their own worst enemies.
university_explanation: Valluvar uses the doubled noun-verb peezhikkum peezhai (பீழிக்கும் பீழை, the affliction with which they afflict) to stress self-made misery, and seruvaar (செறுவார், those who hate, enemies) to set up the comparison. All the modern commentators agree on the sense: the harm fools do to themselves exceeds what an enemy could achieve (Mu. Varadarasanar: ‘of a measure even their foes cannot inflict’; Kalaignar: ‘the torment enemies could not deliver, fools give themselves’). Puliyur Kesigan notes the distress-causing nature (varuththam) of such self-inflicted suffering. The thought links this chapter to the Natpiyal’s concern with enemies: for the fool, the most dangerous enemy is internal. Both web texts read identically.

tamil:
வெண்மை எனப்படுவ தியாதெனின் ஒண்மை
உடையம்யாம் என்னும் செருக்கு.
transliteration:
Venmai enappaduva dhiyaadhenin onmai
udaiyamyaam ennum serukku.
current_meaning: If you ask what stupidity is, it is the arrogance that says, “We are the wise ones.”
elementary_explanation: A kid who says “I already know everything, I don’t need to listen” stops learning right there. The poet says that feeling of being sure you are the smartest is exactly what being foolish means.
university_explanation: The kural defines folly by a pair of light-words: venmai (வெண்மை, literally ‘whiteness’, i.e. blankness, emptiness of mind) is set against onmai (ஒண்மை, ‘brightness’, i.e. keen intelligence). Folly is not mere blankness but the serukku (செருக்கு, conceit, intoxicated pride) that claims brightness: ‘udaiyam yaam’, ‘we possess it’, with the royal or self-inflating plural. Mu. Varadarasanar equates venmai with pullarivu, the chapter’s key term; Pappaiah calls it a ‘delusion’ (mayakkam) and Kalaignar ‘arrogance’ (aanavam). Structurally the kural mirrors 831 in the preceding chapter (‘pedhaimai enbadhondru yaadhenin…’), giving a definition in question-and-answer form. Text identical in both sources.

tamil:
கல்லாத மேற்கொண் டொழுகல் கசடற
வல்லதூஉம் ஐயம் தரும்.
transliteration:
Kallaadha merkon dozhugal kasadara
valladhooum aiyam tharum.
current_meaning: Pretending to know what you never learned makes people doubt even the things you have truly mastered.
elementary_explanation: If a boy who is great at football starts bragging that he is also a chess champion, and everyone sees he can’t play chess, they start wondering whether he is really good at football either. Faking one thing makes people doubt the real things too.
university_explanation: Kallaadha (கல்லாத, what one has not learned) set against kasadara valladhu (கசடற வல்லது, what one has mastered without flaw) gives the kural its hinge, and the emphatic -ooum (‘even that’) shows the reach of the damage: aiyam (ஐயம், doubt) spreads from the pretended to the genuine. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read kallaadha as unread books (nool), so the fool pretends to scholarship; Kalaignar widens it to any field one pretends to know. Puliyur Kesigan reads merkondu ozhugal more actively as rashly undertaking a task one has not learned, which casts doubt even on work one could do perfectly. The kural is a pointed observation about credibility: a single exposed pretense devalues an entire reputation. Both sources give identical text.

tamil:
அற்றம் மறைத்தலோ புல்லறிவு தம்வயின்
குற்றம் மறையா வழி.
transliteration:
Atram maraiththalo pullarivu thamvayin
kutram maraiyaa vazhi.
current_meaning: If you do not get rid of your faults, then carefully covering your body with clothes is itself foolishness.
elementary_explanation: Imagine someone who irons a perfect shirt every morning but is mean to everyone all day. Looking neat on the outside doesn’t hide the meanness. The poet says hiding your body but not fixing your faults is silly.
university_explanation: Atram (அற்றம்) here means the parts of the body to be covered, nakedness; maraiththal is covering it. Valluvar sets this against kutram (குற்றம், fault, moral defect) that remains unhidden (maraiyaa), arguing that modesty about the body while one’s faults stay on display is pullarivu, the very ‘petty understanding’ the chapter is named for. Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all take ‘covering faults’ to mean removing them (neekkuthal), not concealing them, and Puliyur Kesigan adds the image of the hypocrite fully clothed and walking about ‘as though good’. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads atram differently, as ‘ruin’ or ‘loss’, giving a minority interpretation that concealing one’s downfall is the petty act. Text identical in both sources.

tamil:
அருமறை சோரும் அறிவிலான் செய்யும்
பெருமிறை தானே தனக்கு.
transliteration:
Arumarai sorum arivilaan seyyum
perumirai thaane thanakku.
current_meaning: The fool who lets precious counsel slip, whether by ignoring good advice or by failing to guard a vital secret, does great harm to himself.
elementary_explanation: If your coach gives you a secret play and you shout it across the field, or you just forget it because you weren’t listening, your own team loses. The poet says the fool who lets good advice slip away hurts himself most.
university_explanation: The crux is arumarai sorum (அருமறை சோரும்): arumarai is ‘a rare/precious marai’, where marai may mean a secret, a hidden counsel, or a sacred teaching, and sorum means ‘lets slip, lets go loose’. Mu. Varadarasanar follows the traditional reading: the fool fails to keep a precious secret in his mind and blurts it out. Pappaiah and Kalaignar instead read it as failing to accept or follow precious advice, Puliyur Kesigan as studying the rare scriptures yet growing slack and missing their true sense, and Sivayogi Sivakumar as abandoning rare insights. All converge on the second line: perumirai (பெருமிறை, great harm or affliction) is done by the fool thaane thanakku, ‘himself to himself’, echoing 843. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
ஏவவும் செய்கலான் தான்தேறான் அவ்வுயிர்
போஒம் அளவுமோர் நோய்.
transliteration:
Evavum seygalaan thaandheraan avvuyir
poom alavumor noi.
current_meaning: Someone who will not do what is right even when told, and cannot figure it out for himself, is like a disease that lasts until the day he dies.
elementary_explanation: Some kids can figure out on their own to pack their bag; others at least do it when Mum reminds them. But a kid who won’t think of it and won’t listen when told stays stuck forever. The poet says that kind of stubbornness is like a sickness that never goes away.
university_explanation: Valluvar names two routes to right action, being told (evavum, ஏவவும், ‘even when commanded’) and working it out oneself (thaan theral, தான் தேறல், self-ascertainment), and condemns the person who has neither. Such a life is ‘or noi’ (ஓர் நோய், a disease) until the soul departs (poom, the poetic lengthened form of pogum, marked by the alapedai -oom). Commentators differ on whose disease: Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar make it a lifelong affliction for the person himself, while Pappaiah, like the classical gloss reflected in the English ‘a burden (to the earth)’, makes him a disease to the world. Kalaignar’s idiom ‘neither sondha-puththi nor sol-puththi’ (neither one’s own wit nor heeding others’ words) neatly captures the double failure. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
காணாதான் காட்டுவான் தான்காணான் காணாதான்
கண்டானாம் தான்கண்ட வாறு.
transliteration:
Kaanaadhaan kaattuvaan thaankaanaan kaanaadhaan
kandaanaam thaankanda vaaru.
current_meaning: Whoever tries to show the truth to a fool ends up looking like the fool himself, because the fool is sure he already sees everything in his own way.
elementary_explanation: Try explaining to a little brother who is sure the moon follows his car that it only looks that way. He just laughs at you and says you don’t understand. The poet says that when you try to teach someone who is sure he’s right, you end up looking silly.
university_explanation: The kural is a wordplay on kaan (காண், to see): kaanaadhaan (one who does not see) is set against kaattuvaan (one who shows) and kandaan (one who has seen), and the line turns on ‘thaankanda vaaru’ (in the way he himself saw). Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as: one who tries to enlighten a fool becomes a fool himself, while the fool appears wise by his own lights; Pappaiah adds that the fool regards his teacher as the fool. Kalaignar sharpens the second half: the fool shows himself off as wise on the strength of what he alone knows. Puliyur Kesigan gives a different construal: the fool who shows others only what he saw remains one who never saw the truth. The density of the kaan-roots makes the kural famous for its sound-play. Both sources give identical text.

tamil:
உலகத்தார் உண்டென்பது இல்லென்பான் வையத்து
அலகையா வைக்கப் படும்.
transliteration:
Ulagaththaar undenbadhu illenbaan vaiyaththu
alagaiyaa vaikkap padum.
current_meaning: Whoever flatly denies what the wise of the world affirm to be true will be regarded on this earth as a demon and kept apart.
elementary_explanation: If everyone has seen the sun rise every morning and one boy keeps insisting “There is no sun!”, people stop taking him seriously and leave him out of games. The poet says that someone who denies what everyone knows is true gets treated like a spooky outsider.
university_explanation: Ulagaththaar (உலகத்தார்) here, as often in the Kural, means not the crowd but the learned of the world (Pappaiah: ‘the great ones’, uyarndhor), and their ‘undu’ (it exists) is denied by the fool’s ‘il’ (it does not). The traditional commentators gloss what is denied as established truths such as the other world, merit and the divine, attested by the learned; Kalaignar gives a modern secular reading: denying what has been clearly shown with evidence. Such a person is placed (vaikkappadum) as an alagai (அலகை, a demon, ghost or pey) on earth, that is, shunned as something not quite human. Sivayogi Sivakumar and Mu. Varadarasanar both stress exclusion (oduhukkappaduvaan, vilakkappaduvaan). The chapter thus ends with perverse denial as the extreme of pullarivu. Text identical in both sources.

tamil:
இகலென்ப எல்லா உயிர்க்கும் பகலென்னும்
பண்பின்மை பாரிக்கும் நோய்.
transliteration:
Ikalenba ellaa uyirkkum pakalennum
panbinmai paarikkum noi.
current_meaning: The wise call hostility a disease: in every living being it feeds the ugly trait of refusing to get along with others.
elementary_explanation: Think of a bad cold that spreads from one kid in class to everyone. Grudges work the same way: one person stops getting along with another, and soon nobody can play together. The poet says that kind of falling-out is a sickness, and it can catch anyone.
university_explanation: Valluvar opens the chapter with a definition: ikal (இகல், hostility, mental antagonism) is a noi (நோய், disease) that ‘spreads out’ or ‘nourishes’ (paarikkum, பாரிக்கும்) pakal (பகல், separation, non-union) in all creatures. The wordplay is deliberate: pakal normally means ‘daytime’ but here carries its older sense of ‘division’, which Puliyur Kesigan glosses as kūdāmai (கூடாமை, not coming together) and Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘failing to harmonise with other lives’. The traditional commentators following Parimelazhagar treat ikal as the inner root from which outward enmity (pagai, the subject of the next chapter, Pagaimaatchi) grows, which explains why this chapter sits in the Natpiyal (friendship) section of Porutpal. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads ikal unusually as ‘contempt’ (இகழ்ச்சி) that resists another’s nature; Kalaignar emphasises its social result, people unable to live together. The couplet text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பகல்கருதிப் பற்றா செயினும் இகல்கருதி
இன்னாசெய் யாமை தலை.
transliteration:
Pakalkarudhip patraa seyinum ikalkarudhi
innaasey yaamai thalai.
current_meaning: Even if someone, set on breaking with you, does things you dislike, the highest course is not to hurt them in return out of hostility.
elementary_explanation: Suppose a classmate stops being your friend and does mean little things to you. You could plan to get back at them, but the poet says the best thing is not to. Not paying back meanness with meanness is what a really strong person does.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a symmetry of motives: the other person acts pakal karudhi (பகல் கருதி, intending separation) and does patraa (பற்றா, unloving or disagreeable things), while you are warned against acting ikal karudhi (இகல் கருதி, out of hostility) and doing innaa (இன்னா, harmful things). The final word thalai (தலை, ‘head’, foremost) marks this restraint as the supreme course. Puliyur Kesigan and Mu. Varadarasanar both read it as forbearance under provocation; Solomon Pappaiah calls it a ‘superior quality’ (சிறந்த குணம்). The thought echoes the Aram chapters on Innaa Seyyaamai (ch. 32), especially Kural 314, but here it is set in Porutpal as practical statecraft: retaliation turns disagreement into lasting enmity. Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
இகலென்னும் எவ்வநோய் நீக்கின் தவலில்லாத்
தாவில் விளக்கம் தரும்.
transliteration:
Ikalennum evvanoi neekkin thavalillaath
thaavil vilakkam tharum.
current_meaning: If you rid yourself of the painful disease called hostility, it will give you a renown that never fades and never fails.
elementary_explanation: Imagine carrying a heavy, smelly bag of grudges everywhere you go. When you finally drop it, you feel lighter, and people start to remember you as the kind one. The poet says letting go of hostility makes you shine in a way that lasts.
university_explanation: Evvanoi (எவ்வநோய்) is a compound of evvam (எவ்வம், distress, affliction) and noi (disease): hostility is a sickness that torments its host. Its removal yields vilakkam (விளக்கம், literally ‘light, clarity’, here ‘renown, distinction’) qualified twice: thaval illaa (தவல் இல்லா, undiminishing) and thaavil (தாவில், flawless or unfailing). Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read the outcome as imperishable fame (அழியாத புகழ்), Kalaignar as ‘stainless, lasting fame’, while Sivayogi Sivakumar takes vilakkam more literally as inner clarity. The image of illness and cure continues from 851, so the chapter treats hostility medically: diagnosis (851), restraint (852), cure and its fruit (853). Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் பயக்கும் இகலென்னும்
துன்பத்துள் துன்பங் கெடின்.
transliteration:
Inbaththul inbam payakkum ikalennum
thunbaththul thunbang kedin.
current_meaning: When hostility, the worst of all miseries, is destroyed, it yields the greatest of all joys.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever made up with a friend after a big fight? That warm, happy feeling afterwards is one of the best feelings there is. The poet says being angry at someone is the worst kind of unhappy, so ending it brings the best kind of happy.
university_explanation: The couplet is a chiasmus of superlatives: inbaththul inbam (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம், joy among joys) answers thunbaththul thunbam (துன்பத்துள் துன்பம், sorrow among sorrows). The verb payakkum (பயக்கும், yields, produces) makes joy the direct fruit of hostility’s destruction (kedin, கெடின், ‘if it perishes’). Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it straightforwardly as ‘the greatest misery gone, the greatest delight comes’. The same formula ‘துன்பத்துள் துன்பம் கெடின்’ appears in Kural 369 on desire (avaa), so Valluvar ranks hostility alongside craving as the chief sources of suffering. Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
இகலெதிர் சாய்ந்தொழுக வல்லாரை யாரே
மிக்லூக்கும் தன்மை யவர்.
transliteration:
Ikaledhir saaindhozhuka vallaarai yaare
mikalookkum thanmai yavar.
current_meaning: Who could ever hope to overcome those who are able to turn away from hostility whenever it rises in them?
elementary_explanation: Picture someone trying to start a fight with a kid who just smiles and won’t fight back. After a while, there is nothing to fight about, and the bully gives up. The poet says nobody can beat a person who never lets anger take over.
university_explanation: The key phrase is ikal edhir saaindhu ozhuga (இகல் எதிர் சாய்ந்து ஒழுக): to ‘lean away against’ hostility, i.e. to recoil from it and conduct oneself in the opposite direction when it arises within. Puliyur Kesigan specifies ‘when hostility arises in one’s own heart’, so the victory is first over oneself; mikal ūkkum (to aspire to overcome) then describes would-be conquerors, of whom ‘who’ (yaare) implies none. Textual note: both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print the second line as ‘மிக்லூக்கும்’ while their own romanizations read ‘mikalookkum’ and thirukkural.net’s song version prints ‘மிகலூக்கும்’; the word is mikal + ūkkum, and the printed form appears to be a shared digital orthographic slip. The same form recurs in 858. The text is otherwise identical in both sources.

tamil:
இகலின் மிகலினிது என்பவன் வாழ்க்கை
தவலும் கெடலும் நணித்து.
transliteration:
Ikalin mikalinidhu enbavan vaazhkkai
thavalum kedalum naniththu.
current_meaning: For the one who says it is sweet to get ahead through hostility, failure and ruin are close at hand.
elementary_explanation: Some people enjoy picking fights because winning feels good. But someone who always looks for a fight soon has no friends and lots of enemies, and things start to go wrong fast. The poet warns that loving fights leads to falling down.
university_explanation: Ikalin mikal inidhu (இகலின் மிகல் இனிது): ‘to excel (mikal) by means of hostility is sweet’ is the boast of the quarrelsome man. Valluvar answers that for him thavalum (தவலும், failing, slipping) and kedalum (கெடலும், perishing) are naniththu (நணித்து, near). Puliyur Kesigan reads mikal as ‘exceeding others in hostility’, Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘victory through hostility’, and Kalaignar as ‘thinking victory easy through opposition’. Pappaiah gives a distinctive reading: such a life’s survival is brief, and its ruin also comes within a brief time. The couplet turns from the inner disease to its social consequence. Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
மிகல்மேவல் மெய்ப்பொருள் காணார் இகல்மேவல்
இன்னா அறிவி னவர்.
transliteration:
Mikalmeval meypporul kaanaar ikalmeval
innaa arivi navar.
current_meaning: Those whose harmful minds are bent on hostility can never see the true principle that leads to success.
elementary_explanation: When you are really angry at someone, it is hard to think clearly, a bit like trying to read with foggy glasses. The poet says people who love fighting have foggy minds, so they miss the smart, true way to win.
university_explanation: The couplet balances two uses of mēval (மேவல், attaching to, desiring): ikal mēval (attachment to hostility) and mikal mēval (attaining victory). Those with innaa arivu (இன்னா அறிவு, a harmful or grievous intellect) who cling to hostility cannot see meypporul (மெய்ப்பொருள், the true substance or principle) of success. Puliyur Kesigan and Solomon Pappaiah identify this ‘true substance’ with nīti nūl porul, the teaching of the treatises on statecraft, so hostility blinds a ruler to sound policy; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it more generally as ‘the truth that leads to victory’. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead splits the couplet into two statements about pride and hostility. Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
இகலிற்கு எதிர்சாய்தல் ஆக்கம் அதனை
மிக்லூக்கின் ஊக்குமாம் கேடு.
transliteration:
Ikalirku edhirsaaidhal aakkam adhanai
mikalookkin ookkumaam kedu.
current_meaning: Turning away from hostility brings prosperity; whoever pushes it further invites ruin to hurry toward him.
elementary_explanation: A small fire can be stamped out, but if you keep feeding it sticks it grows until it burns the house. The poet says anger is like that: put it out and good things grow, feed it and trouble comes running.
university_explanation: The first line repeats the key verb of 855, edhir saaidhal (எதிர் சாய்தல், to lean away from), now naming its reward: aakkam (ஆக்கம், prosperity, growth). The second line plays on ūkkam (ஊக்கம், urging, zeal): if one urges hostility on (mikal ūkkin), ruin ‘urges itself’ (ūkkumaam kēdu) toward that person, an elegant mirroring. Puliyur Kesigan reads the first line as checking hostility before it rises in one’s own heart; Pappaiah as ‘not welcoming’ it; Kalaignar as confronting and removing it. Textual note: as in 855, both base sources print ‘மிக்லூக்கின்’ while ytamizh romanizes ‘miklookkin’; the morphology is mikal + ūkkin, and the printed cluster looks like a shared digital slip. Otherwise identical.

tamil:
இகல்காணான் ஆக்கம் வருங்கால் அதனை
மிகல்காணும் கேடு தரற்கு.
transliteration:
Ikalkaanaan aakkam varungaal adhanai
mikalkaanum kedu thararku.
current_meaning: When good fortune is coming, a person does not think of hostility; when he is bringing ruin on himself, he looks to magnify it.
elementary_explanation: When you are having a great day, a small bump does not bother you. But on a bad day, you might turn a tiny bump into a huge fight that makes everything worse. The poet says growing a quarrel is a sign that trouble is on its way.
university_explanation: The couplet reads hostility as a symptom of one’s turning fortune. Ikal kaanaan (இகல் காணான், ‘does not regard hostility’) when aakkam (prosperity) is coming; but to bring on kēdu (கேடு, ruin) he mikal kaanum (மிகல் காணும், ‘sees its increase’, magnifies it). Puliyur Kesigan and Pappaiah add that the fortunate man ignores hostility even with cause, while the one heading for ruin seeks it even without cause. Mu. Varadarasanar reads mikal as ‘seeking to win against it’. The underlying idea, that a mind inclines toward quarrel when its own fall is approaching, resembles the Sanskrit maxim vināśa-kāle viparīta-buddhi (‘at the time of ruin the mind turns perverse’), though Valluvar states it without fatalism. Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
இகலானாம் இன்னாத எல்லாம் நகலானாம்
நன்னயம் என்னும் செருக்கு.
transliteration:
Ikalaanaam innaadha ellaam nakalaanaam
nannayam ennum serukku.
current_meaning: From hostility come all painful things; from friendliness comes the proud wealth called true goodness.
elementary_explanation: Grumpy, fighting groups have lots of problems, while friendly groups share, help, and feel proud of each other. The poet ends the chapter simply: fighting brings every kind of trouble, and friendship brings goodness you can be proud of.
university_explanation: The closing couplet sets ikal against nakal (நகல், literally ‘laughing together’, hence friendship, cordiality). From ikal come innaadha ellaam (இன்னாத எல்லாம், all that is painful); from nakal comes nannayam ennum serukku (நன்னயம் என்னும் செருக்கு), ‘the elation called great good’. Puliyur Kesigan and Mu. Varadarasanar gloss nannayam as nalla nīti (good justice or policy) and serukku as perumidha nilai (a state of dignified pride); Pappaiah renders it ‘the wealth-pride of justice’, while Kalaignar reads it as ‘great joy’. Serukku usually means arrogance in the Kural, so its positive use here is notable: the only pride worth having is the dignity friendship confers. Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக ஓம்பா
மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை.
transliteration:
Valiyaarkku maaretral ombuka ombaa
meliyaarmel meka pakai.
current_meaning: Refrain from setting yourself against those stronger than you; but do not shrink from taking up enmity against those who are weaker.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a small boat and a giant ship. A smart small boat does not try to bump the giant ship, because it would sink. Valluvar says: pick your contests wisely, and never start a fight you cannot possibly win.
university_explanation: The chapter title pakai maatchi (பகை மாட்சி) means the ‘excellence’ or right conduct of enmity: not whether a ruler will have enemies, but which enmities are worth having. The couplet turns on a deliberate wordplay between ombuka (ஓம்புக, ‘guard against, avoid’) and ombaa (ஓம்பா, ‘without avoiding’), and on meka (மேக, from mevu, ‘desire, take up’). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read it as plain statecraft: avoid opposing the stronger, and willingly take up enmity against the weaker; Solomon Pappaiah sharpens it to ‘if weaker, attack at once’. Mu. Karunanidhi (Kalaignar) notably inverts the moral, praising the one who spares the weak and fights the strong as the true glory of enmity, a modern ethical rereading rather than the traditional gloss. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அன்பிலன் ஆன்ற துணையிலன் தான்துவ்வான்
என்பரியும் ஏதிலான் துப்பு.
transliteration:
Anbilan aandra thunaiyilan thaanthuvvaan
enpariyum edhilaan thuppu.
current_meaning: One who has no love for his own people, no strong allies, and no strength of his own: how could he ever break the power of an enemy?
elementary_explanation: Think of a team captain who is mean to his teammates, has no friends on other teams to help, and is not a strong player himself. When a tough team shows up, how can he possibly win? Kindness, friends and your own strength are what keep you safe.
university_explanation: The couplet lists three deficits: anbilan (அன்பிலன், without love, which Pappaiah and Varadarasanar read as lacking affection for kin and subjects), aandra thunaiyilan (ஆன்ற துணையிலன், without worthy or powerful allies) and thaan thuvvaan (தான் துவ்வான், himself lacking strength). The closing phrase enpariyum edhilaan thuppu (என் பரியும் ஏதிலான் துப்பு) asks how such a man could destroy (pari) the strength (thuppu) of a stranger-foe (edhilaan). Parimelazhagar reads the verse as the converse of 861: such a person is himself the ‘weak’ party whom others may safely oppose. The trio of affection, alliance and own strength mirrors the Arthashastra’s concern with internal loyalty and allies (mitra) as elements of royal power. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அஞ்சும் அறியான் அமைவிலன் ஈகலான்
தஞ்சம் எளியன் பகைக்கு.
transliteration:
Anjum ariyaan amaivilan eekalaan
thanjam eliyan pakaikku.
current_meaning: A man who is fearful, ignorant, unable to get along with others and unwilling to give is utterly easy prey for his enemies.
elementary_explanation: Picture a kid who is scared of everything, doesn’t learn the rules of the game, won’t cooperate with anyone, and never shares. When trouble comes, nobody stands with him and he doesn’t know what to do. Being brave, learning, getting along and sharing are what make you strong.
university_explanation: Four faults are stacked in quick succession: anjum (அஞ்சும், he who fears, which Pappaiah glosses as fearing what need not be feared), ariyaan (அறியான், one who does not know what should be known), amaivilan (அமைவிலன், lacking accord or adaptability with others) and eekalaan (ஈகலான், one who does not give). Thanjam (தஞ்சம்) is read by the commentators as an intensifier, ‘very easily’ (Varadarasanar: மிக எளியவன்). Parimelazhagar’s logic is cumulative: fear loses battles, ignorance loses policy, unsociability loses allies and stinginess loses the army, so the foe has little left to overcome. Kalaignar renders amaivilan as lacking the habit of living in harmony and eekalaan as lacking compassion. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நீங்கான் வெகுளி நிறையிலன் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
யாங்கணும் யார்க்கும் எளிது.
transliteration:
Neengaan vekuli niraiyilan enjnaandrum
yaanganum yaarkkum elidhu.
current_meaning: One whose anger never leaves him and who has no inner restraint is easy for anyone to defeat, at any time and in any place.
elementary_explanation: If a player gets angry every time and can’t keep the team’s plan a secret, the other team just has to tease him and listen in. He makes himself easy to beat. Staying calm and keeping your plans to yourself is a kind of armour.
university_explanation: Neengaan vekuli (நீங்கான் வெகுளி) is anger that does not depart, a settled irascibility rather than a passing flare. Nirai (நிறை) is the key term: Varadarasanar glosses it as the capacity to hold and govern one’s own mind, while Parimelazhagar’s tradition, followed by Solomon Pappaiah and the classic English rendering (‘neither refrains from anger nor keeps his secrets’), reads it as guarding secrets. Both senses describe a leak in self-command through which the enemy can enter. The triple universal of the second line, enjnaandrum yaanganum yaarkkum (எஞ்ஞான்றும் யாங்கணும் யார்க்கும், at all times, in all places, to all), makes the vulnerability total. This anticipates chapter 31 (vekulaamai, avoiding anger), here recast as political danger. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
வழிநோக்கான் வாய்ப்பன செய்யான் பழிநோக்கான்
பண்பிலன் பற்றார்க்கு இனிது.
transliteration:
Vazhinokkaan vaayppana seyyaan pazhinokkaan
panbilan patraarkku inidhu.
current_meaning: One who does not look to the right path, does not do what is fitting, does not care about disgrace and has no good character is a delight to his enemies.
elementary_explanation: A kid who never reads the rules, doesn’t do his homework, doesn’t care if people think badly of him and isn’t kind is very easy for a rival to beat. His rival is actually happy to face him! Learning the right way and caring about your good name make you hard to beat.
university_explanation: Vazhi nokkaan (வழிநோக்கான்) is glossed by Parimelazhagar’s tradition, and by Puliyur Kesigan and Pappaiah, as one who does not study the treatises of right conduct (neethi nool); Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it more broadly as not seeking the good path. Vaayppana seyyaan (வாய்ப்பன செய்யான்) is one who fails to do what those texts enjoin or what is fitting; pazhi nokkaan (பழிநோக்கான்) disregards blame or disgrace; panbilan (பண்பிலன்) lacks character. Patraar (பற்றார்) are ‘those who do not hold to him’, that is, enemies, and inidhu (இனிது, sweet) is deliberately ironic: such a man is a pleasure to fight. The sequence moves from knowledge to action to reputation to character. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
காணாச் சினத்தான் கழிபெருங் காமத்தான்
பேணாமை பேணப் படும்.
transliteration:
Kaanaach chinaththaan kazhiperung kaamaththaan
penaamai penap padum.
current_meaning: The enmity of a man blinded by anger and swollen with boundless desire is something to be welcomed, because he will defeat himself.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a rival who gets so angry he can’t see straight and wants everything he sees, right now. He runs around grabbing and shouting and forgets to defend himself. Having a rival like that is almost lucky, because his own temper and greed trip him up.
university_explanation: Kaanaach chinam (காணாச் சினம்) is anger that does not see, which Puliyur Kesigan explains as anger that blinds one to oneself and to others, and Varadarasanar as anger that does not see the truth. Kazhi perung kaamam (கழிபெருங் காமம்) is desire grown beyond all measure; Pappaiah specifies it as lust for women, while Varadarasanar and Kalaignar keep the broader sense of greed or great desire. The second line plays on the root penu (to cherish): penaamai (பேணாமை, non-cherishing, i.e. enmity) penap padum (பேணப் படும், will be cherished), so his hostility is ‘to be prized’ by others. The pairing of krodha and kama as twin enemies of self-government is common to classical Indian thought. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் மன்ற அடுத்திருந்து
மாணாத செய்வான் பகை.
transliteration:
Koduththum kolalvendum mandra aduththirundhu
maanaadha seyvaan pakai.
current_meaning: The enmity of one who stays close to you yet does what is unworthy should certainly be had, even if you must pay a price for it.
elementary_explanation: Suppose someone on your own team keeps quietly messing up every play. It would honestly be better if he went over to the other team, even if you had to give up something to make that happen. A clear opponent is safer than a teammate who harms you from inside.
university_explanation: The commentators divide on aduththirundhu (அடுத்திருந்து). Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as ‘staying close by’: one who remains near you as an associate yet does unworthy things (maanaadha, மாணாத) should be turned into an open enemy, even at the cost of wealth. The older line represented by Parimelazhagar, followed by Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesigan and by the classic English version (‘having begun a work, does what is not conducive’), reads it as ‘having undertaken’ an action: the enmity of a foe who mismanages his own undertakings is so advantageous that it is worth buying. Mandra (மன்ற) means ‘certainly’. Either way the paradox is that some enmity is a gain worth paying for. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
குணனிலனாய்க் குற்றம் பலவாயின் மாற்றார்க்கு
இனனிலனாம் ஏமாப் புடைத்து.
transliteration:
Gunanilanaayk kutram palavaayin maatraarkku
inanilanaam emaap pudaiththu.
current_meaning: A man with no virtues and many faults ends up with no allies, and that very friendlessness becomes a strength for his enemies.
elementary_explanation: If someone is never kind and always does mean things, little by little all his friends leave. When a problem comes, he is alone, and that makes it easy for anyone against him. Good habits are what keep friends by your side.
university_explanation: The couplet is a causal chain: gunanilan (குணனிலன், without good qualities) plus kutram pala (குற்றம் பல, many faults) yields inanilan (இனனிலன், one without kin or allies, from inam, ‘one’s own group’), and that condition is emaappu (ஏமாப்பு, security or advantage) for the maatraar (மாற்றார், adversaries). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah both stress that it is the friendlessness itself, not any action of the foe, that becomes the enemy’s strength. Kalaignar condenses this to ‘he loses his supporters and is easily brought down’. The verse links this chapter back to the Natpiyal chapters on friendship that precede it. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
செறுவார்க்குச் சேணிகவா இன்பம் அறிவிலா
அஞ்சும் பகைவர்ப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Seruvaarkkuch chenikavaa inbam arivilaa
anjum pakaivarp perin.
current_meaning: Those who fight will never be far from joy if they happen to get enemies who are both foolish and fearful.
elementary_explanation: If you are playing a game and your opponent doesn’t understand the rules and is scared to make any move, winning becomes easy and fun. Valluvar says a foolish, frightened enemy is really a stroke of luck for the other side.
university_explanation: Seruvaar (செறுவார்) are those who attack or contend; sen ikavaa inbam (சேண் இகவா இன்பம்) is joy that does not go far away, i.e. abiding delight. Varadarasanar keeps this sense (pleasures will not depart), while Puliyur Kesigan reads it as ‘all lofty pleasures remain with them’. The enemy’s two qualities, arivilaa (அறிவிலா, without understanding, which Pappaiah specifies as without knowledge of what is just) and anjum (அஞ்சும், fearing), recapitulate the first two faults of 863. Kalaignar renders the joy specifically as the joy of victory. The verse is the offensive counterpart to the chapter’s earlier defensive lists. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கல்லான் வெகுளும் சிறுபொருள் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
ஒல்லானை ஒல்லா தொளி.
transliteration:
Kallaan vekulum siruporul enjnaandrum
ollaanai ollaa tholi.
current_meaning: The man who will not take even the small, easy gain of opposing an unlearned foe will never have glory come to him.
elementary_explanation: If you won’t even try an easy level of a game, how will you ever beat the hard ones and earn a trophy? Valluvar says that someone who shies away from small, easy challenges never earns a great name.
university_explanation: The syntax is compressed: kallaan vekulum siruporul (கல்லான் வெகுளும் சிறுபொருள்) is ‘the small gain of being angry with (fighting) the unlearned man’, and ollaanai ollaadhu oli (ஒல்லானை ஒல்லாது ஒளி) says that light, i.e. fame, will not unite with the one who does not obtain it. Varadarasanar on thirukkural.net reads: one who cannot do the easy thing of opposing the unlearned will never gain glory; Pappaiah adds that the gain from fighting one ignorant of the treatises is small, yet the king who disdains it earns no renown; Kalaignar has fame mock such a man for hesitating even before untrained foes. Note: ytamizh.com’s Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar glosses for 870 are misplaced (they discuss forgiving old friends, the theme of kural 810); the couplet text itself is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பகைஎன்னும் பண்பி லதனை ஒருவன்
நகையேயும் வேண்டற்பாற்று அன்று.
transliteration:
Pakaiennum panpi ladhanai oruvan
nakaiyeyum ventarpaatru andru.
current_meaning: Enmity is a thing with no goodness in it; no one should wish for it, not even as a game or a joke.
elementary_explanation: Some kids pretend to be enemies just for fun, teasing and picking fights as a joke. The poet says even pretend enmity is a bad game, because a joke fight can quickly turn into a real one that nobody can stop.
university_explanation: The chapter opens by naming its subject with a moral label: pakai (பகை, enmity) is panpiladhu (பண்பிலது), ‘that which is devoid of good quality’. The emphatic nakaiyeyum (நகையேயும், ‘even in jest / even in play’) carries the force of the couplet: enmity is not to be courted even in sport, still less in earnest. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as an evil without merit that should not be desired even as a pastime, and Kalaignar explains that enmity runs contrary to good character; Puliyur Kesigan adds that this is the settled conclusion of the ethical treatises. The placement is notable: in a chapter that goes on to give hard-headed advice about handling enemies, Valluvar first insists that enmity itself is never desirable. The text is identical in ytamizh and thirukkural.net, which titles the chapter பகைத்திறந் தெரிதல் with a word break.

tamil:
வில்லேர் உழவர் பகைகொளினும் கொள்ளற்க
சொல்லேர் உழவர் பகை.
transliteration:
Viller uzhavar pakaikolinum kollarka
soller uzhavar pakai.
current_meaning: Even if you must make enemies of warriors whose plough is the bow, never make enemies of the wise whose plough is the word.
elementary_explanation: A bully with big muscles can only hurt you while he is near you. But a clever person who writes and speaks well can tell your story to the whole town and to people years from now. So the poet says: if you must quarrel with anyone, never quarrel with the people who are good with words.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a celebrated agricultural metaphor: villēr uḻavar (வில்லேர் உழவர்) are ‘ploughmen whose plough is the bow’, that is, warriors, while collēr uḻavar (சொல்லேர் உழவர்) are ‘ploughmen whose plough is the word’. Mu. Varadarasanar reads the latter as scholars, Solomon Pappaiah as writers, Kalaignar as learned people of verbal power; the older commentarial tradition, reflected in Pope’s gloss ‘ministers whose ploughs are words’, takes them as counsellors skilled in policy. The concessive kolinum (‘even if you incur’) does not recommend war with soldiers; it ranks dangers, implying that the harm of hostile counsel, satire or reputation outlasts and outreaches the harm of arms. The metaphor also suggests that both kinds of men ‘cultivate’ a harvest, and the harvest of words is wider. No variant readings appear between ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஏமுற் றவரினும் ஏழை தமியனாய்ப்
பல்லார் பகைகொள் பவன்.
transliteration:
Emur ravarinum ezhai thamiyanaaip
pallaar pakaikol pavan.
current_meaning: A person who stands alone and still makes enemies of many is more foolish than someone who has lost their mind.
elementary_explanation: Picture one kid on the playground who has no friends on his side, yet goes around picking fights with every group. Even someone who is not thinking clearly would not do that. The poet says this is the silliest thing a person can do.
