university_explanation: The comparison turns on ēmuṟṟavar (ஏமுற்றவர்), ‘those who are deluded or deranged’: Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah gloss them as the mad (பித்தர்), Kalaignar as the arrogant, while Sivayogi Sivakumar reads ‘the despised’. Ēḻai (ஏழை) here means ‘senseless, witless’, not ‘poor’, as all the commentators agree. Tamiyaṉāy (‘being alone’) and pallār (‘many’) set up the arithmetic: a man without allies who collects many enemies has made the one choice even a madman might avoid. Pappaiah applies it directly to a ruler (ஆட்சியாளன்), in keeping with the Porutpal setting. The text matches in both ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பகைநட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும் பண்புடை யாளன்
தகைமைக்கண் தங்கிற்று உலகு.
transliteration:
Pakainatpaak kontozhukum panputai yaalan
thakaimaikkan thangitru ulaku.
current_meaning: The world rests secure in the greatness of the gracious person who turns enemies into friends and lives that way.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a kid who gets pushed by someone, and instead of pushing back, invites that person to play and they become best friends. The poet says people like that are so great that the whole world is held together by them.
university_explanation: After three couplets warning against enmity, Valluvar names the ideal: the paṇpuṭaiyāḷaṉ (பண்புடையாளன், ‘man of noble character’) who conducts himself (oḻukum) by making pakai into naṭpu (நட்பு, friendship). Takaimai (தகைமை) is greatness or excellence, and taṅkiṟṟu ulaku (‘the world abides’) is a strong claim: the stability of the world itself depends on such people. Mu. Varadarasanar speaks of the world resting in his magnanimity; Solomon Pappaiah reads it of a ruler who converts enemies and lives with them, so that the world falls within his greatness; Kalaignar has the whole world praising such a person; Sivayogi Sivakumar says the world endures through such honoured conduct. Pope renders it as ‘worthy rule can change his foes to friends’, keeping the political frame. The couplet links back to Chapter 87 and forward to the strategic advice in 875.

tamil:
தன்துணை இன்றால் பகையிரண்டால் தான்ஒருவன்
இன்துணையாக் கொள்கவற்றின் ஒன்று.
transliteration:
Thandhunai indraal pakaiyirantaal thaanoruvan
indhunaiyaak kolkavatrin ondru.
current_meaning: If you have no ally, face two enemies, and stand alone, make one of those two enemies into a friendly ally.
elementary_explanation: Suppose two bigger kids are both upset with you and nobody is on your side. Instead of fighting both, you make peace with one of them, and suddenly it is two against one in your favour. That is the smart move the poet recommends.
university_explanation: This is the most explicitly strategic couplet of the chapter. Three conditions are stacked in clipped clauses: taṉtuṇai iṉṟāl (‘if one has no support’), pakai iraṇṭāl (‘if the enemies are two’), tāṉ oruvaṉ (‘and one is alone’). The remedy is to take one of the two as iṉtuṇai (இன்துணை), a ‘sweet’ or agreeable ally. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as a general maxim, while Solomon Pappaiah again frames it for a ruler; Sivayogi Sivakumar keeps it close to the text. It complements 874: where that couplet praised turning enemies into friends as a virtue, this one treats it as a necessity of statecraft, in line with the Indian political tradition of alliances among neighbouring powers. The text is identical in both sources.

tamil:
தேறினும் தேறா விடினும் அழிவின்கண்
தேறான் பகாஅன் விடல்.
transliteration:
Therinum theraa vitinum azhivinkan
theraan pakaaan vital.
current_meaning: Whether or not you have tested and trusted a person before, in a time of crisis neither commit yourself to them nor break with them; keep a careful middle distance.
elementary_explanation: When something big goes wrong, it is not the time to suddenly make a new best friend or to start a new fight. The poet says: stay polite and keep a bit of distance, and wait until things are calm before deciding who to trust.
university_explanation: This is among the most compressed and debated couplets of the chapter. The verb tēṟu (தேறு, ‘to trust, be convinced about’) appears three times: tēṟiṉum tēṟā viṭiṉum (‘whether one has trusted him or not’), then tēṟāṉ (‘not trusting’) paired with pakāaṉ (பகாஅன், ‘not separating’, with the alapedai lengthening), ending in viṭal (‘leave him so’). Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as: whether you had earlier assessed a man or not, in a time of ruin neither trust him nor drop him; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar apply it specifically to an enemy, advising neither closeness nor open rupture; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as ‘do not approach the untrustworthy in ruinous times’. Pope’s verse is loose, and his explanation ‘neither to join nor separate’ follows the traditional reading. The thirukkural.net English summary, ‘be wary of joining or opposing any’, captures the consensus: in crisis, keep a guarded neutrality. The text matches in both sources.

tamil:
நோவற்க நொந்தது அறியார்க்கு மேவற்க
மென்மை பகைவர் அகத்து.
transliteration:
Novarka nondhadhu ariyaarkku mevarka
menmai pakaivar akaththu.
current_meaning: Do not tell your troubles to those who do not already know of them, and do not show weakness in front of your enemies.
elementary_explanation: If you are feeling hurt, you do not have to tell everyone you meet. And if someone is being mean to you, try not to show them where it hurts, because they might poke you there again. Share your worries with the people who really care and already understand.
university_explanation: The couplet has two prohibitions in parallel: nōvaṟka (‘do not lament’) to those who do not know one’s suffering, and mēvaṟka (‘do not take on, display’) meṉmai (மென்மை, ‘softness, weakness’) in the presence of enemies. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take the first line as referring to friends who have not themselves perceived one’s distress: to complain to them is undignified and spreads knowledge of one’s weakness. Solomon Pappaiah reads the hidden object of both lines as ‘our lack of strength’, which should neither be told to unaware friends nor shown to enemies. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads the lines quite differently: do not grieve over those who do not understand grief, and do not covet the soft spot of enemies. Pope’s ‘To those who know them not, complain not of your woes; nor to your foeman’s eyes infirmities disclose’ follows the majority reading. The text is identical in both sources.

tamil:
வகையறிந்து தற்செய்து தற்காப்ப மாயும்
பகைவர்கண் பட்ட செருக்கு.
transliteration:
Vakaiyarindhu tharseydhu tharkaappa maayum
pakaivarkan patta serukku.
current_meaning: Know the right way to act, build up your own strength, and guard yourself well; then the arrogance of your enemies will fade away by itself.
elementary_explanation: If a team keeps teasing yours, the best answer is not to shout back but to practise, get stronger, and play smart. When they see how ready you are, their boasting stops on its own.
university_explanation: Three participial steps lead to the result: vakai aṟintu (‘knowing the method’), taṟceytu (‘making oneself strong’), taṟkāppa (‘guarding oneself’); then māyum (‘will perish’) the cerukku (செருக்கு, ‘pride, arrogance, exultation’) that has arisen in the enemies. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read cerukku as the enemy’s pride, which collapses without a blow once one is prepared; Solomon Pappaiah adds that taṟkāppa includes guarding one’s secrets, linking back to 877; Pope’s explanation renders cerukku as the foes’ ‘joy’ and taṟceytu as ‘securing assistance’, a reading that ties the couplet to 875. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as knowing one’s qualifications and self-protection. The point is deterrence: preparation defeats an enemy’s confidence before any conflict. The text matches in both sources.

tamil:
இளைதாக முள்மரம் கொல்க களையுநர்
கைகொல்லும் காழ்த்த இடத்து.
transliteration:
Ilaidhaaka mulmaram kolka kalaiyunar
kaikollum kaazhththa itaththu.
current_meaning: Cut down a thorny tree while it is still young; once it has hardened, it will wound the hand of the one who tries to remove it.
elementary_explanation: A tiny thorny weed in the garden can be pulled out with two fingers. If you leave it for a year, it grows big, tough thorns that scratch your hands when you finally try to pull it. Problems are the same: deal with them while they are small.
university_explanation: The couplet is a pure agricultural image applied to enmity, as all the commentators make explicit: iḷaitāka (‘while young’) muḷmaram (முள்மரம், ‘thorn tree’) kolka (‘destroy’); otherwise, kāḻtta iṭattu (‘when it has hardened’, from kāḻ, the hard heartwood) it kai kollum (‘destroys the hand’) of the kaḷaiyunar (களையுநர், ‘those who weed it out’). Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the literal image; Kalaignar draws the lesson that enmity must be put down before it matures; Sivayogi Sivakumar adds the explicit note that enmity must not be allowed to grow. Solomon Pappaiah reads the thorn tree as one who intends to destroy us. The verb kol- (‘kill’) appears in both lines, giving a pointed reversal: kill it, or it kills your hand. The text matches in both sources.

tamil:
உயிர்ப்ப உளரல்லர் மன்ற செயிர்ப்பவர்
செம்மல் சிதைக்கலா தார்.
transliteration:
Uyirppa ularallar mandra seyirppavar
semmal sidhaikkalaa thaar.
current_meaning: Those who fail to break the pride of hostile enemies certainly cannot be said to live, not even to the extent of drawing breath.
elementary_explanation: If someone keeps bullying a group and nobody ever stands up to them, the bully only gets bolder. The poet says that people who never stand up to proud, hostile enemies are not really living freely at all.
university_explanation: The closing couplet is the chapter’s sharpest. Uyirppa (உயிர்ப்ப, ‘so much as to breathe’) uḷar allar (‘they do not exist’) maṉṟa (மன்ற, ‘certainly’): such people are not alive even to breathe. The condition is that they cannot citaikkal (‘shatter’) the cemmal (செம்மல், ‘pride, eminence, haughtiness’) of ceyirppavar (செயிர்ப்பவர், ‘those who are hostile or offend’). Kalaignar reads it as: those who cannot break the enemies’ arrogance cannot truly be called alive just because they breathe; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as a prediction that such people will be destroyed within a breath; Mu. Varadarasanar’s printed gloss on ytamizh reads ‘தலைமையைக் கொடுக்க’, which appears to be a typographic slip for கெடுக்க (‘destroy’). Sivayogi Sivakumar takes ceyirppavar as open wrongdoers. Read with 871 and 874, the chapter’s logic is clear: never seek enmity, convert it where possible, but where it persists, deal with it decisively. The text matches in both sources.

tamil:
நிழல்நீரும் இன்னாத இன்னா தமர்நீரும்
இன்னாவாம் இன்னா செயின்.
transliteration:
Nizhalneerum innaadha innaa thamarneerum
innaavaam innaa seyin.
current_meaning: Shade and water are comforts, yet they become harmful when they breed sickness; in the same way, the closeness of one's own people becomes painful when they do harm.
elementary_explanation: A shady tree and a cool drink are lovely on a hot day, but if the water is dirty it can make you sick. Family and friends are meant to be like shade and water, so when someone close to us starts hurting us, it feels even worse than a stranger doing it.
university_explanation: The chapter opens with a paired simile: nizhal-neer (நிழல்நீர், shade and water), the archetypal comforts of a hot land, are innaadha (இன்னாத, painful) when innaa (இன்னா, harmful, i.e. disease-bearing); so too thamar-neer (தமர்நீர், the 'nature' or disposition of one's kin) becomes innaavaam when it does harm. The wordplay on neer, meaning both 'water' and 'nature/quality', is deliberate and is reflected in Mu. Varadarasanar's and Kalaignar's glosses, which read thamar-neer as the qualities of kinsfolk. Solomon Pappaiah extends thamar to one's own party or faction, showing how modern commentators read utpakai (உட்பகை, enmity from within) politically as well as domestically. In the traditional reading framed by Parimelazhagar, the Porul section addresses a ruler, so the 'kin' include courtiers and relations around the throne. Text is identical in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
வாள்போல பகைவரை அஞ்சற்க அஞ்சுக
கேள்போல் பகைவர் தொடர்பு.
transliteration:
Vaalpola pakaivarai anjarka anjuka
kelpol pakaivar thotarpu.
current_meaning: Do not fear enemies who come openly like a drawn sword; fear instead the company of enemies who pose as kinsmen or friends.
elementary_explanation: A bully who shouts at you from across the playground is easy to spot and avoid. The trickier problem is someone who pretends to be your friend while secretly trying to get you in trouble, so that is the person to be careful about.
university_explanation: The couplet sets two kinds of foe against each other: vaal-pola pakaivar (வாள்போல பகைவர், foes like a sword), whose hostility is open and therefore manageable, and kel-pol pakaivar (கேள்போல் பகைவர், foes who appear as kel, 'kin' or intimates). The imperative pair anjarka / anjuka (அஞ்சற்க / அஞ்சுக, 'fear not' / 'fear') gives the verse its antithetical snap. What is to be feared is their thodarpu (தொடர்பு), the ongoing association, since closeness is the very channel through which the hidden enemy works. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the second group as those who behave like relatives while harbouring utpakai, and Pope renders them 'foes who seem like kinsmen'. The text agrees in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உட்பகை அஞ்சித்தற் காக்க உலைவிடத்து
மட்பகையின் மாணத் தெறும்.
transliteration:
Utpakai anjiththar kaakka ulaivitaththu
matpakaiyin maanath therum.
current_meaning: Fear the enemy within and guard yourself, for in a moment of weakness it will cut you down as surely as the potter's tool cuts through clay.
elementary_explanation: A potter uses a thin wire or blade to slice through soft clay in one easy stroke. Hidden enemies wait for a time when you are tired or in trouble, and then they can hurt you just as easily, so it is wise to watch out for them early.
university_explanation: The verse pairs a command, utpakai anji thar kaakka (உட்பகை அஞ்சித் தற்காக்க, 'fearing internal enmity, guard yourself'), with a warning about timing: ulaividaththu (உலைவிடத்து), 'at the time of tottering' or decline. The image matpakai (மட்பகை), literally 'clay-enemy', is glossed by Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar as the potter's cutting tool that slices clay vessels, so that maana therum (மாணத் தெறும்) means 'will destroy thoroughly'. Pope's 'potter's knife' follows the same reading. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead reads the second line as setting a cooking pot on an unfired clay vessel, an interpretive variant rather than a textual one. The Tamil text is identical in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மனமாணா உட்பகை தோன்றின் இனமாணா
ஏதம் பலவும் தரும்.
transliteration:
Manamaanaa utpakai thondrin inamaanaa
edham palavum tharum.
current_meaning: If hidden enmity arises in a mind that will not be reformed, it brings many troubles that turn one's own people against one.
elementary_explanation: If a person keeps a secret grudge and refuses to let it go, it slowly spoils everything around them. Soon brothers, sisters and friends are arguing and taking sides, and the whole group stops getting along.
university_explanation: The verse balances two negated compounds: mana-maanaa (மனமாணா, 'mind not made excellent', i.e. unreformed or unreconciled) and ina-maanaa (இனமாணா, 'kin not made excellent', i.e. kinsfolk who fall out of harmony). When utpakai arises in the first, it yields edham palavum (ஏதம் பலவும், many faults or evils) of the second kind. Mu. Varadarasanar reads the result as many faults that keep one's kin from being set right, while Kalaignar says such a disposition makes one's own people into enemies. Pope's 'secret enmities ... that minds pervert' and the thirukkural.net rendering 'myriad miseries manifest among kin' both preserve the link between inner hostility and outer estrangement. No textual variant is attested between ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உறல்முறையான் உட்பகை தோன்றின் இறல்முறையான்
ஏதம் பலவும் தரும்.
transliteration:
Uralmuraiyaan utpakai thondrin iralmuraiyaan
edham palavum tharum.
current_meaning: If hidden enmity arises among those bound by kinship, it brings many deadly evils.
elementary_explanation: When a family has a big fight that nobody fixes, it can grow worse and worse until it breaks the family apart. The poet says a quarrel inside the family can be the most dangerous kind of all.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on a chiming pair: ural-muraiyaan (உறல்முறையான், 'by way of relationship') and iral-muraiyaan (இறல்முறையான், 'by way of death'). Where enmity springs from kinship, it yields evils of a deadly kind. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as 'many sufferings of the kind that kill', and Solomon Pappaiah as 'many faults joined with death'. Pope's explanation speaks of internal hatred 'in a (king's) family' leading to 'fatal crime', showing the royal framing of the traditional commentary, where kin-enmity means dynastic feud. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads iral-muraiyaan differently, as harm extending even to those outside the kin, an interpretive variant. The Tamil text agrees in both sources.

tamil:
ஒன்றாமை ஒன்றியார் கட்படின் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
பொன்றாமை ஒன்றல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Ondraamai ondriyaar katpatin egngnaandrum
pondraamai ondral aridhu.
current_meaning: Once discord takes hold among those who were united, it is ever hard to escape destruction.
elementary_explanation: Think of a team that always played together well. If the players start secretly disliking each other, they stop passing the ball and stop helping, and soon even an easy match is lost. Once a group splits, it is very hard to stop it from falling apart.
university_explanation: The couplet is a study in the root ondru (ஒன்று, 'to be one, to unite'): ondraamai (ஒன்றாமை, disunity) arises among ondriyaar (ஒன்றியார், those who were united), and then pondraamai ondral (பொன்றாமை ஒன்றல், 'attaining non-perishing', i.e. escaping ruin) becomes aridhu (அரிது, difficult) egngnaandrum (எஞ்ஞான்றும், at any time). Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as: when enmity arises among one's own people, it is always hard to avoid perishing through that internal enmity; Solomon Pappaiah applies it to a government whose fall cannot then be prevented. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as the difficulty of ever reuniting once a group is split by another's intrigue. Both sources print the same text, and thirukkural.net transliterates katpatin, reflecting the sandhi of kan + padin.

tamil:
செப்பின் புணர்ச்சிபோல் கூடினும் கூடாதே
உட்பகை உற்ற குடி.
transliteration:
Seppin punarchchipol kootinum kootaadhe
utpakai utra kuti.
current_meaning: A family gripped by hidden enmity may look joined like a casket and its lid, yet it is never truly united.
elementary_explanation: A box and its lid fit together neatly, but they are still two separate pieces that can be pulled apart at any moment. A family that is secretly angry inside may look together at dinner, but deep down they are not really united.
university_explanation: The governing image is seppin punarchchi (செப்பின் புணர்ச்சி, 'the joining of a seppu'), a small casket whose lid sits flush on its body so that the two look like one object. A kudi (குடி, family, clan or community) that has suffered utpakai may koodinum (கூடினும், even though it comes together) yet kootaadhu (கூடாதே, will surely not unite). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read seppu as a lidded casket, and Pope translates 'casket with its cover'. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead reads seppu as copper used to join two different metals, an interpretive variant. Pappaiah extends kudi to the party and the state. The text is identical in both sources.

tamil:
அரம்பொருத பொன்போலத் தேயும் உரம்பொருது
உட்பகை உற்ற குடி.
transliteration:
Aramporudha ponpolath theyum uramporudhu
utpakai utra kuti.
current_meaning: A family afflicted by internal enmity wears itself down, its strength rubbed away, like metal worn by a file.
elementary_explanation: When you rub a file back and forth on a piece of metal, a little dust falls off each time until the metal gets thinner and thinner. A family that keeps fighting inside loses a little strength every day in the same way, until there is not much left.
university_explanation: The image is aram porudha pon (அரம் பொருத பொன், metal struck by a file), which theyum (தேயும், wears away). The second line, uram porudhu (உரம் பொருது), means that the family's own strength (uram) is ground away by the friction of utpakai. Pon usually means gold, as Pope and thirukkural.net render it, but Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss it as iron (இரும்பு), reflecting the wider sense of pon as metal. The echo of porudha / porudhu (struck / striking) emphasises that the family is both the file and the metal, wearing itself down. The text agrees in both sources.

tamil:
எட்பக வன்ன சிறுமைத்தே ஆயினும்
உட்பகை உள்ளதாங் கேடு.
transliteration:
Etpaka vanna sirumaiththe aayinum
utpakai ulladhaang ketu.
current_meaning: Even if internal enmity is as small as a split sesame seed, ruin lies within it.
elementary_explanation: A sesame seed is one of the tiniest seeds there is, and half a seed is smaller still. The poet says even a grudge that small, kept hidden inside a group, can grow until it breaks everything apart.
university_explanation: The measure of smallness is etpakavu (எட்பகவு, the split half of a sesame seed), among the tiniest units in Tamil idiom; anna (அன்ன) means 'like'. However sirumaiththu (சிறுமைத்து, slight) the utpakai is, ketu (கேடு, ruin) is ulladhu (உள்ளது, present) within it. Mu. Varadarasanar says that even at that size it carries ruin able to destroy a whole family, and Solomon Pappaiah reads it as destruction already present inside the faction. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead reads 'ulladhu' as 'all that exists', giving 'ruin to everything', a reading the word order allows. The thirukkural.net rendering ('even a dissent as small as a seed') and Pope ('slight as shred of sesame seed') agree with the dominant reading. The text is identical in both sources.

tamil:
உடம்பாடு இலாதவர் வாழ்க்கை குடங்கருள்
பாம்போடு உடனுறைந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Utampaatu ilaadhavar vaazhkkai kutangarul
paampotu utanurain thatru.
current_meaning: Living together with those who are not truly in agreement with you is like sharing a small hut with a snake.
elementary_explanation: Imagine sleeping in a tiny tent with a snake curled up in the corner. You could never relax, because you would always be wondering when it might bite. Living with someone who secretly dislikes you feels the same way.
university_explanation: The closing couplet gives the chapter its most vivid image. Utampaatu ilaadhavar (உடம்பாடு இலாதவர்) are 'those without inner agreement', people who share one's life without sharing one's mind. To live with them is kutangarul paampotu utanurainthatru (குடங்கருள் பாம்போடு உடனுறைந்தற்று), 'like dwelling together with a snake inside a kutangar'. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah gloss kutangar as a small hut (குடிசை), and Kalaignar stresses the moment-by-moment fear of such a life. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as a dark cave, an interpretive variant. Pope's 'dwelling in a shed with snake for company' and thirukkural.net's 'share a hut with a cobra' agree on the hut reading. The text is identical in both sources.

tamil:
ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் இகழாமை போற்றுவார்
போற்றலுள் எல்லாம் தலை.
transliteration:
Aatruvaar aatral ikazhaamai potruvaar
potraluL ellaam thalai.
current_meaning: Of all the precautions a careful person can take to protect themselves, the first and best is never to belittle the strength of those who are able to accomplish what they set out to do.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a small puppy barking and nipping at a big, calm elephant. The safest thing the puppy can do is simply not tease the elephant. Being respectful to people who are strong and capable is the best way to keep yourself out of trouble.
university_explanation: The opening couplet frames the whole adhikaram as a matter of self-protection: poatruvaar (போற்றுவார், those who guard themselves) have many kinds of poatral (போற்றல், guarding, watchfulness), but the thalai (தலை, head, foremost) of them all is ikazhaamai (இகழாமை, not despising) the aatral (ஆற்றல், power, capability) of aatruvaar (ஆற்றுவார், those able to carry out what they undertake). Pope’s explanation, following the traditional commentary associated with Parimelazhagar, reads the chapter in the setting of statecraft: having discussed internal enmity (Ch. 89), Valluvar now warns the king and his men against offending two classes of the great, the mighty in worldly power and the great in spiritual power (ascetics). Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both gloss aatruvaar as one able to complete a chosen task, while Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as those who lead and guide. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பெரியாரைப் பேணாது ஒழுகிற் பெரியாரால்
பேரா இடும்பை தரும்.
transliteration:
Periyaaraip penaadhu ozhukir periyaaraal
peraa itumpai tharum.
current_meaning: If a person conducts himself without showing due regard to the great, that very disregard will bring him lasting, irremovable trouble at their hands.
elementary_explanation: If you keep ignoring your coach and being rude, you might find yourself benched for the whole season. Not treating important people with respect can bring trouble that doesn’t go away quickly.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on the repeated periyaar (பெரியார், the great): conduct (ozhugal, ஒழுகல்) that does not penu (பேணு, cherish, honour) the great yields, through those same great ones, peraa idumbai (பேரா இடும்பை, affliction that does not depart). The adjective peraa (from pe-, to move away) stresses permanence, which Mu. Varadarasanar renders as நீங்காத துன்பம். Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it simply as disrespect to elders or great persons, while the traditional reading behind Pope’s explanation glosses periyaar as powerful rulers. The phrase periyaaraal (by the great) shows that the harm is not mere fate but the active response of the offended party. Both sources agree on the text, including the sandhi form ஒழுகிற்.

tamil:
கெடல்வேண்டின் கேளாது செய்க அடல்வேண்டின்
ஆற்று பவர்கண் இழுக்கு.
transliteration:
Ketalventin kelaadhu seyka atalventin
aatru pavarkan izhukku.
current_meaning: If a person wants to bring ruin on himself, let him, without heeding anyone, commit offences against those who are able to destroy whenever they wish.
elementary_explanation: If you poke a sleeping bear with a stick and ignore everyone shouting stop, you are asking for trouble. Valluvar says, with a wink: if you want to get hurt, go ahead and annoy the strongest one around.
university_explanation: This couplet uses irony: keDal veNDin (கெடல் வேண்டின், if you desire ruin), keLaadhu seyga (கேளாது செய்க, do it without listening), izhukku (இழுக்கு, offence, fault) toward aatrupavar (ஆற்றுபவர், those able) aDal veNDin (அடல் வேண்டின், when they wish to slay). The phrase keLaadhu is read differently: Pope’s explanation, following the traditional commentary, takes it as not listening to the righteous dictates of law or the nīti texts, and Solomon Pappaiah likewise speaks of ignoring what the moral treatises say; Kalaignar reads it as not listening to anyone’s advice; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads the first half more freely as a separate clause. The pairing keDal/aDal is a typical Valluvar sound-echo. The text is identical in both sources, which print ஆற்று பவர்கண் with the metrical split.

tamil:
கூற்றத்தைக் கையால் விளித்தற்றால் ஆற்றுவார்க்கு
ஆற்றாதார் இன்னா செயல்.
transliteration:
Kootraththaik kaiyaal viliththatraal aatruvaarkku
aatraadhaar innaa seyal.
current_meaning: When the powerless do harm to the powerful, it is like beckoning Death with one’s own hand to come and take them.
elementary_explanation: A tiny mouse that pulls a lion’s tail is basically waving and calling, Come and get me! When someone weak picks a fight with someone much stronger, they are inviting their own trouble.
university_explanation: The image is vivid: kootram (கூற்றம், Death, Yama, the god who divides life from body) is summoned kaiyaal viLiththu (கையால் விளித்து, by beckoning with the hand). The comparison applies to aatraadhaar (ஆற்றாதார், those without power) doing innaa (இன்னா, harm) to aatruvaar (ஆற்றுவார், the powerful). Solomon Pappaiah specifies the three kinds of power, of wisdom, wealth and army, and adds that it is the weak who strike first; Mu. Varadarasanar stresses that Yama would come of himself anyway, so the weak only hasten it. The couplet carries forward kural 891’s key word aatruvaar, binding the chapter together. Text is the same in both sources.

tamil:
யாண்டுச்சென்று யாண்டும் உளராகார் வெந்துப்பின்
வேந்து செறப்பட் டவர்.
transliteration:
Yaantuchchendru yaantum ularaakaar vendhuppin
vendhu serappat tavar.
current_meaning: Those who have earned the anger of a king of fierce strength will not survive anywhere, wherever they may flee.
elementary_explanation: Playing hide-and-seek with someone who can see everywhere is no fun, because there is nowhere to hide. If you make a very powerful ruler angry, no hiding place is safe.
university_explanation: Here the great one is a vendhu (வேந்து, king) of vem-thuppu (வெந்துப்பு, fierce strength); those seRappaTTavar (செறப்பட்டவர், who have incurred his wrath, from seRu, to be angry) will be uLar aakaar (உளர் ஆகார், will not exist, will not live) yaaNDu senRu yaaNDum (wherever they go, anywhere). Solomon Pappaiah and Mu. Varadarasanar agree that the offender cannot live anywhere; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads uLar aakaar more psychologically, as being unable to settle. Pope’s rendering notes they will not prosper wherever they go. The two sources agree on the text; thirukkural.net’s transliteration shows the metrical division வெந்துப்பின் / வேந்து, with the split செறப்பட் டவர் in both.

tamil:
எரியால் சுடப்படினும் உய்வுண்டாம் உய்யார்
பெரியார்ப் பிழைத்தொழுகு வார்.
transliteration:
Eriyaal sutappatinum uyvuntaam uyyaar
periyaarp pizhaiththozhuku vaar.
current_meaning: Someone caught and burnt by fire may still survive, but those who go on offending the great will not escape.
elementary_explanation: Getting burnt by a campfire hurts, but you can heal. Valluvar says that hurting truly great people is even more dangerous than fire, because there may be no getting better from it.
university_explanation: The comparison is a fortiori: eri (எரி, fire) can burn a man and still uyvu uNDaam (உய்வு உண்டாம், there may be escape, survival), but uyyaar (உய்யார், they will not survive) who periyaarp pizhaiththu ozhuguvaar (பெரியார்ப் பிழைத்து ஒழுகுவார், live in offence against the great). The chapter title itself comes from this root, pizhai (பிழை, fault, offence). Pope’s explanation, reflecting the traditional commentary, glosses the fire as a forest fire and the great as devotees or ascetics, whose spiritual power is pictured as more consuming than physical flame. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the great as those of surpassing power generally. The text is the same in both sources.

tamil:
வகைமாண்ட வாழ்க்கையும் வான்பொருளும் என்னாம்
தகைமாண்ட தக்கார் செறின்.
transliteration:
Vakaimaanta vaazhkkaiyum vaanporulum ennaam
thakaimaanta thakkaar serin.
current_meaning: If the truly worthy, eminent in character, turn their anger on someone, what use is that person’s splendid life and vast wealth?
elementary_explanation: You could have the biggest toy collection in the world, but if you are mean to the kindest, wisest grown-up in town, everyone will stop trusting you. All your toys can’t fix that. Good people’s goodwill is worth more than riches.
university_explanation: Two pairs balance each other: vagai maaNDa vaazhkkai (வகைமாண்ட வாழ்க்கை, a life excellent in every kind) and vaan poruL (வான்பொருள், sky-high wealth) are worth ennaam (என்னாம், what will they become?) if thagai maaNDa thakkaar (தகைமாண்ட தக்கார், the worthy, distinguished in noble quality) seRin (செறின், are angered). Pope’s explanation, following the traditional commentary, applies this to a king whose government with all its auxiliaries and untold wealth is useless before the wrath of the righteous great; Solomon Pappaiah glosses the great as those excellent in character. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads the couplet differently, as saying that wealth and splendour cannot equal the richness of the worthy, showing an alternative interpretation of seRin. Both sources print the same text.

tamil:
குன்றன்னார் குன்ற மதிப்பின் குடியொடு
நின்றன்னார் மாய்வர் நிலத்து.
transliteration:
Kundrannaar kundra madhippin kutiyotu
nindrannaar maaivar nilaththu.
current_meaning: If those who are great like mountains are held in low esteem, or resolve on someone’s ruin, even people who seemed permanently established will perish from the earth together with their families.
elementary_explanation: Think of a mountain: it is big, steady and old. If you try to knock a mountain down, you will only hurt yourself. People who are great like mountains deserve respect, and those who treat them badly can lose everything, even their family’s good name.
university_explanation: The couplet plays on kunRu (குன்று, hill, mountain) and kunRa (குன்ற, to diminish): if kunRannaar (குன்றன்னார், those like mountains) are kunRa madhikkap paDin (thought of as diminished, slighted), or, in another reading, if they madhi (மதி, resolve) on diminishing someone, then even ninRannaar (நின்றன்னார், those who seem to stand forever) maaivar (மாய்வர், will perish) kuDiyoDu (குடியொடு, along with their lineage) nilaththu (நிலத்து, on earth). The two readings are visible in the commentaries: Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take it as the mountain-like great resolving on destruction, while Sivayogi Sivakumar and Kalaignar take it as others belittling the great. Pope’s explanation, following the traditional commentary, identifies the mountain-like ones as devotees. The text is identical in both sources.

tamil:
ஏந்திய கொள்கையார் சீறின் இடைமுரிந்து
வேந்தனும் வேந்து கெடும்.
transliteration:
Endhiya kolkaiyaar seerin itaimurindhu
vendhanum vendhu ketum.
current_meaning: When those who uphold lofty principles rise in anger, even a king will be broken midway and lose his kingdom.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a team captain who bullies the fairest, most honest player. When the whole team sees it and stands with that honest player, the captain loses the job. Even powerful people can fall if they anger those who live by high principles.
university_explanation: Eendhiya koLgaiyaar (ஏந்திய கொள்கையார்) are those who bear aloft high principles or vows; if they seeRin (சீறின், flare up in anger), even the vendhan (வேந்தன், king) will iDai murindhu (இடை முரிந்து, be broken midway) and vendhu keDum (வேந்து கெடும், his kingship will perish). Pope’s explanation glosses the king as Indra and the great as those of exalted vows, reflecting the traditional commentary’s allusion to Nahusha, who was cast down from Indra’s throne by the curse of the sage Agastya. Modern commentators generalize: Solomon Pappaiah speaks of a ruler losing office midway, and Kalaignar reads it politically as tyranny collapsing when principled people rise up. The text is identical in both sources.

tamil:
இறந்தமைந்த சார்புடையர் ஆயினும் உய்யார்
சிறந்தமைந்த சீரார் செறின்.
transliteration:
Irandhamaindha saarputaiyar aayinum uyyaar
sirandhamaindha seeraar serin.
current_meaning: Even those who have boundless support and powerful allies cannot escape if people of outstanding greatness are angered against them.
elementary_explanation: Having lots of friends to stick up for you is great, but if you do something really wrong to a truly good and respected person, even all those friends can’t save you. Being respectful is better protection than having a big gang.
university_explanation: The final couplet sets iRandhu amaindha saarbu (இறந்தமைந்த சார்பு, supports exceeding all measure, from iRa, to go beyond) against siRandhu amaindha seeraar (சிறந்தமைந்த சீரார், those whose glory is excellently formed). The verb uyyaar (உய்யார், they will not survive) echoes kural 896, and seRin (செறின், if angered) echoes 895 and 897, rounding off the chapter. Pope’s explanation, following the traditional commentary, glosses the great here as the noble whose penance is boundless, so the chapter ends where it began, with the two kinds of greatness, worldly and spiritual. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads iRandhamaindha as like the dead, that is renunciants, a markedly different interpretation of the first phrase. Both sources agree on the text.
